# solana_program_option - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-option/

## Expand description

A C representation of Rust’s `Option`, used across the FFI
boundary for Solana program interfaces.

This implementation mostly matches `std::option` except iterators since the iteration
trait requires returning `std::option::Option`

- A C representation of Rust’s `std::option::Option`

# solana_nullable - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-nullable/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

Types for values that can reserve a designated null value.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Maybe](https://docs.rs/struct.MaybeNull.html)- Null
- A wrapper that can be used as an `Option<T>`without requiring extra space to indicate whether the value is`Some`or`None`.

- Error type for invalid `MaybeNull`conversions.

- Trait for types that can be `None`.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# repose_ui - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/repose-ui/0.21.1/repose_ui/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#views-modifiers-and-layout)Views, Modifiers, and Layout

Repose UI is built around three core ideas:

- `View`: an immutable description of a UI node.
- `Modifier`: layout, styling, and interaction hints attached to a- `View`.
- Layout + paint: a separate pass (`layout_and_paint`) that turns the`View`tree into a`Scene`+ hit regions using the Taffy layout engine.

[§](https://docs.rs#views)Views

A `View` is a lightweight value that describes *what* to show, not *how* it is
rendered. It is cheap to create and you are expected to rebuild the entire
view tree on each frame:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use repose_core::*;
use repose_ui::*;
fn Counter(count: i32, on_inc: impl Fn() + 'static) -> View {
    Column(Modifier::new().padding(16.0)).child((
        Text(format!("Count = {count}")),
        Button("Increment".into_children(), on_inc),
    ))
}
```
Internally, a `View` has:

- `id: ViewId`- assigned during composition/layout.
- `kind: ViewKind`- which widget it is (Text, Button, ScrollV, etc.).
- `modifier: Modifier`- layout/styling/interaction metadata.
- `children: Vec<View>`- owned child views.

Views are *pure data*: they do not hold state or references into platform
APIs. State lives in signals / `remember_*` and platform integration happens
in the runner (`repose-platform`).

[§](https://docs.rs#modifiers)Modifiers

`Modifier` describes *how* a view participates in layout and hit‑testing:

- Size hints: `size`,`width`,`height`,`min_size`,`max_size`,`fill_max_size`,`fill_max_width`,`fill_max_height`.
- Box model: `padding`,`padding_values`.
- Visuals: `background`,`background_brush`,`border`,`clip_rounded`,`alpha`,`transform`.
- Flex / grid: `flex_grow`,`flex_shrink`,`flex_basis`,`align_self`,`justify_content`,`align_items`,`grid`,`grid_span`.
- Positioning: `absolute()`,`offset(..)`for overlay / Stack / FABs.
- Interaction: `clickable()`, pointer callbacks,`on_scroll`,`semantics`.
- Custom paint: `painter`(used by`repose-canvas`).

Example:

```
use repose_core::*;
use repose_ui::*;
fn CardExample() -> View {
    Box(
        Modifier::new()
            .padding(16.0)
            .background(theme().surface)
            .border(1.0, theme().outline, 8.0)
            .clip_rounded(8.0),
    )
    .child(Text("Hello, Repose!"))
}
```
Modifiers are merged into a Taffy `Style` inside `layout_and_paint`. Most
values are specified in density‑independent pixels (dp) and converted to
physical pixels (`px`) using the current `Density` local.

[§](https://docs.rs#layout-1)Layout

Layout is a pure function:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
pub fn layout_and_paint(
    root: &View,
    size_px: (u32, u32),
    textfield_states: &HashMap<u64, Rc<RefCell<TextFieldState>>>,
    interactions: &Interactions,
    focused: Option<u64>,
) -> (Scene, Vec<HitRegion>, Vec<SemNode>);
```
It:

- Clones the root `View`and assigns stable`ViewId`s.
- Builds a parallel Taffy tree and computes layout for the given window size.
- Walks the tree to:
- Emit `SceneNode`s for visuals (rects, text, images, scrollbars, etc.).
- Build `HitRegion`s for input routing (clicks, pointer events, scroll).
- Build `SemNode`s for accessibility / semantics.

- Emit

`Row`, `Column`, `Stack`, `Grid`, `ScrollV` and `ScrollXY` are all special
`ViewKind`s that map into Taffy styles and additional paint/hit logic.

Because layout + paint are separate from the platform runner, you can reuse the same UI code on desktop, Android, and other platforms.

# repose_tree - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/repose-tree/0.21.1/repose_tree/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#repose-tree)repose-tree

Persistent view tree with incremental reconciliation.

Instead of rebuilding the entire view tree every frame, this module maintains a persistent tree structure that:

- **Stable Identity**: Nodes have stable IDs across frames
- **Change Detection**: Content hashing identifies what changed
- **Incremental Updates**: Only changed subtrees are processed
- **Layout Caching**: Unchanged nodes keep their cached layout

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ ViewTree │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│ │ nodes: SlotMap<NodeId, TreeNode> ││
│ │ root: NodeId ││
│ │ dirty: FxHashSet<NodeId> ││
│ │ generation: u64 ││
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
│
▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ TreeNode │
│ ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐│
│ │ id: NodeId ││
│ │ view_id: ViewId (stable user-facing ID) ││
│ │ kind: ViewKind ││
│ │ modifier: Modifier ││
│ │ children: SmallVec<[NodeId; 4]> ││
│ │ parent: Option<NodeId> ││
│ │ content_hash: u64 ││
│ │ layout_cache: Option<LayoutCache> ││
│ │ generation: u64 ││
│ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘│
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Layout](https://docs.rs/struct.LayoutCache.html)- Cache
- Cached layout information for a node.
- [Layout](https://docs.rs/struct.LayoutConstraints.html)- Constraints
- Constraints used during layout.
- [NodeId](https://docs.rs/struct.NodeId.html)
- Internal node identifier, stable within a tree’s lifetime.
- [Reconcile](https://docs.rs/struct.ReconcileContext.html)- Context
- Context for a reconciliation pass.
- [Tree](https://docs.rs/struct.TreeNode.html)- Node
- A node in the persistent view tree.
- [Tree](https://docs.rs/struct.TreeStats.html)- Stats
- Statistics about tree operations.
- [View](https://docs.rs/struct.ViewTree.html)- Tree
- A persistent view tree that supports incremental updates.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [hash_](https://docs.rs/fn.hash_subtree.html)- subtree
- Compute a hash that includes the subtree structure. This combines the node’s content hash with its children’s subtree hashes.
- [hash_](https://docs.rs/fn.hash_view_content.html)- view_ - content
- Compute a content hash for a View’s immediate properties. This does NOT include children - that’s handled separately.

# repose_text - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/repose-text/0.21.1/repose_text/

Look up the CacheKey for a GlyphKey and extract outline commands in one engine lock.
Returns None if the GlyphKey isn’t in the key map or extraction fails.

Like wrap_lines, but returns byte ranges into the original text
for each visual line. This is required for multi-line editing so
caret/selection mapping stays correct.

Greedy wrap into lines that fit max_width. Prefers breaking at whitespace,
falls back to grapheme boundaries. If max_lines is Some and we truncate,
caller can choose to ellipsize the last visible line.

# repose_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/repose-core/0.21.1/repose_core/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#state-signals-and-effects)State, Signals, and Effects

Repose uses a small reactive core instead of an explicit widget tree with mutable fields. There are three main pieces:

- `Signal<T>`- observable, reactive value.
- `remember*`- lifecycle‑aware storage bound to composition.
- `effect`/- `scoped_effect`- side‑effects with cleanup.

[§](https://docs.rs#signals)Signals

`Signal<T>` is a cloneable handle to a piece of state:

```
use repose_core::*;
let count = signal(0);
count.set(1);
count.update(|v| *v += 1);
assert_eq!(count.get(), 2);
```
Reads participate in a dependency graph: when you call `get()` inside an
observer or `produce_state`, future writes will automatically recompute that
observer.

[§](https://docs.rs#remembered-state)Remembered state

UI state is typically held in `remember_*` slots rather than globals:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use repose_core::*;
fn CounterView() -> View {
    let count = remember_state(|| 0); // Rc<RefCell<i32>>
    let on_click = {
        let count = count.clone();
        move || *count.borrow_mut() += 1
    };
    repose_ui::Button(
        format!("Count = {}", *count.borrow()),
        on_click,
    )
}
```
- `remember`and- `remember_state`are order‑based: the Nth call in a composition slot always refers to the Nth stored value.
- `remember_with_key`and- `remember_state_with_key`are key‑based and more stable across conditional branches.

[§](https://docs.rs#derived-state)Derived state

`produce_state` computes a `Signal<T>` from other signals and recomputes it
automatically when dependencies change:

```
use repose_core::*;
let first = signal("Jane".to_string());
let last  = signal("Doe".to_string());
let full = produce_state("full_name", {
    let first = first.clone();
    let last  = last.clone();
    move || format!("{} {}", first.get(), last.get())
});
assert_eq!(full.get(), "Jane Doe");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#effects-and-cleanup)Effects and cleanup

Use `effect` / `scoped_effect` for one‑off side‑effects with cleanups:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use repose_core::*;
fn Example() -> View {
    scoped_effect(|| {
        log::info!("Mounted Example");
        on_unmount(|| log::info!("Unmounted Example"))
    });
    // ...
    repose_ui::Box(Modifier::new())
}
```
- `effect`runs once when the view is composed and returns a- `Dispose`guard that will be run when the scope is torn down.
- `scoped_effect`is wired to the current- `Scope`and is cleaned up on scope disposal (e.g. when a navigation entry is popped).

For long‑running tasks (network, timers), prefer building small helpers on
top of `scoped_effect` so everything cleans up correctly when the UI that
owns it disappears.

# arcx-cli

CLI scaffolding tool for **Arcx** — a convention-over-configuration web framework for Rust.

## Install

```
```
## Commands

### Create a new project

```
```
Generated structure:

```
myapp/
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs
│   ├── router.rs
│   ├── prelude.rs
│   ├── controller/
│   │   └── home.rs
│   ├── middleware/
│   ├── service/
│   │   ├── mod.rs        # services! container
│   │   └── user.rs
│   ├── schedule/
│   └── helper/
│       └── response.rs
├── config/
│   ├── config.default.toml
│   └── config.prod.toml
└── Cargo.toml
```
### Generate code (auto-register)

All generators automatically register into the appropriate files — zero manual wiring.

```
# Generate controller (alias: g c)
# → Creates src/controller/user.rs
# → Auto-registers in controller/mod.rs + router.rs
# Generate service (alias: g s)
# → Creates src/service/order.rs
# → Auto-registers in service/mod.rs (services! macro)
# Generate middleware (alias: g m)
# → Creates src/middleware/rate_limit.rs (Ctx + Next + ReqParts signature)
# → Auto-registers in middleware/mod.rs
# Generate schedule job (alias: g j)
# → Creates src/schedule/cleanup.rs
# → Auto-registers in schedule/mod.rs + main.rs (.schedule())
```
### Development server (hot reload)

```
```
Watches file changes, recompiles, and restarts automatically.

```
```
## Configuration

Each middleware/feature manages its own config section:

```
# config/config.default.toml
[]
 = 3000
[]
 = true
 = ["*"]
[]
 = true
[]
 = true
 = false
```
Rule: **has section +  enable = true = on.** No section or

`enable = false` = off.## Links

- [arcx-macros](https://crates.io/crates/arcx-macros)— Proc macros

# jammi_wire - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jammi-wire/0.32.1/jammi_wire/

## Expand description

The Jammi gRPC wire substrate.

`jammi-wire` is the candle-free home for everything both sides of the
`jammi.v1` wire share: the generated tonic stubs ([ proto](https://docs.rs/proto/index.html)), the
proto↔domain conversions, the request / eval / fine-tune vocabulary the
conversions map, the Arrow-IPC framing helpers, and the

[the typed clients build their per-service stubs over.](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionTransport.html)

`SessionTransport`Both sides of the wire live here so the conversions compile once and are used
in both directions: the prost types are local to this crate (generated by
`build.rs`) and the domain types are local too (the moved vocabulary and the
`jammi-db` substrate), so `From`/`TryFrom` impls satisfy the orphan rule
without a newtype wrapper. `jammi-server` consumes the server stubs + these
conversions; `jammi-admin` / `jammi-client` consume the client stubs + the
same conversions — neither reimplements a mapping.

Arrow record batches cross the wire through the IPC-stream helpers
([ encode_ipc_stream](https://docs.rs/fn.encode_ipc_stream.html) /

[), which carry a self-describing IPC stream (schema + batches) in one](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_ipc_stream.html)

`decode_ipc_stream``ArrowBatch.data_body` — the Flight-IPC
pairing the trigger, inference, and mutable-table surfaces share.## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [eval](https://docs.rs/eval/index.html)
- Evaluation vocabulary: the transport-neutral report shapes and task/shape enums every eval consumer shares.
- [fine_](https://docs.rs/fine_tune/index.html)- tune
- Fine-tune request vocabulary: the transport-neutral config + method types.
- [proto](https://docs.rs/proto/index.html)
- Proto-generated types for the `jammi.v1`API surface.
- [request](https://docs.rs/request/index.html)
- Request vocabulary the consumer surface shares with the wire.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Eval](https://docs.rs/struct.EvalTaskFromWire.html)- Task - From - Wire
- Carries the decoded engine `EvalTask``impl TryFrom<i32> for EvalTask`collides with`core`’s blanket`TryFrom<T> for T`(the compiler cannot prove`EvalTask != i32`across crates), so the conversion lands on this local marker; the handler unwraps`.0`.
- [Proto](https://docs.rs/struct.ProtoQueryInput.html)- Query - Input
- The proto query oneof paired with its resolved `Modality``text`, IMAGE/AUDIO require`data`(raw bytes); a missing oneof or a mismatch is a client error.
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionHeader.html)- Header
- Injects the `SESSION_HEADER``SessionTransport`
- [Session](https://docs.rs/struct.SessionTransport.html)- Transport
- A connected gRPC transport scoped to one client session.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [FILE_](https://docs.rs/constant.FILE_DESCRIPTOR_SET.html)- DESCRIPTOR_ - SET
- The compiled `jammi.v1`proto`FileDescriptorSet`, emitted by`build.rs`.
- [SESSION_](https://docs.rs/constant.SESSION_HEADER.html)- HEADER
- Header name carrying the opaque session identifier. Clients mint a per-connection id and include it on every request that needs tenant-scoped semantics; the server’s session store keys the tenant binding by it. One definition shared by both sides so the header name cannot drift.

- Decode the `data_header`+`data_body`of an`ArrowBatch`into the record batches it carries. Concatenates the two byte runs (the trigger pairing puts the schema header inline in`data_body`and leaves`data_header`empty, but a producer may split them) and reads every batch from the resulting IPC stream. Inverse of`encode_ipc_stream`
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_publish_batch.html)- publish_ - batch
- Decode the single record batch a `Publish`carries, checking it against the topic schema. Per ADR-01 §5.1 the wire pairing is`data_header`+`data_body`; the shared decoder concatenates them and reads the IPC stream. A publish carries exactly one batch — an empty or multi-batch payload is a typed client error, and a schema mismatch is rejected so a malformed publish never partially writes.
- [decode_](https://docs.rs/fn.decode_subscribed_batch.html)- subscribed_ - batch

The wire body is tenant-free (a list entry’s tenant rides the session scope, not the message), so the engine definition reconstructs with`tenant = None`; a list consumer keys off the id / schema / primary key / indexes, not the catalog row’s tenant. # jammi-cli 0.32.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/jammi-cli/0.32.1

# jammi-cli

Command-line interface for [Jammi AI](https://github.com/f-inverse/jammi-ai).

A strict gRPC client: `jammi` talks to a running `jammi-server` over the wire
(`--target`) and never touches the catalog or storage in-process. Manage data
sources, run SQL queries, and drive the trigger / channel / mutable-table
surfaces from your terminal.

## Install

```
```
## Usage

```
# Point at a running server (default --target is grpc://127.0.0.1:8081)
# Report server capabilities and confirm reachability
# Register a data source
# Query with SQL
# Show execution plan
# List sources and models
```
Run the server itself with the `jammi-server` binary (or a container image),
not this CLI.

## Documentation

See the [Jammi AI Guide](https://f-inverse.github.io/jammi-ai/) for the full guide.

## License

Apache-2.0

# jammi_client - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/jammi-client/0.32.1/jammi_client/

## Expand description

The Jammi data-plane client.

[ DataClient](https://docs.rs/struct.DataClient.html) is the network peer of the embedded session for the data
verbs: SQL (over Flight SQL), embeddings / encode / search, inference,
fine-tune submit + status, the eval verbs, the trigger publish / subscribe
surface, and audit. It composes a

[over the](https://docs.rs/jammi-admin/0.32.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jammi_admin/struct.CatalogClient.html)

`jammi_admin::CatalogClient`*same*

[for the control verbs and the tenant trio, so a tenant bound through](https://docs.rs/jammi-wire/0.32.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/jammi_wire/transport/struct.SessionTransport.html)

`jammi_wire::SessionTransport``bind_tenant` is observed by every data verb
on the same session id. It is candle-free — it speaks the gRPC + Flight SQL
wire only and pulls no embedded engine.Three properties make it interchangeable with the embedded session:

- **Faithful errors.**Every failure decodes the structured- `jammi_wire`- *exact*- `jammi_db::error::JammiError`
- **Tenant over the wire.**The tenant trio rides the composed- `CatalogClient`- `SESSION_HEADER`
- **Shared conversions.**Request encode / response decode reuse the- `jammi_wire`

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Data](https://docs.rs/struct.DataClient.html)- Client
- A data-plane client backed by a remote engine over gRPC + Flight SQL.

# solana_program_option - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-option/3.1.0/target-redirect/solana_program_option/

## Expand description

A C representation of Rust’s `Option`, used across the FFI
boundary for Solana program interfaces.

This implementation mostly matches `std::option` except iterators since the iteration
trait requires returning `std::option::Option`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [COption](https://docs.rs/enum.COption.html)
- A C representation of Rust’s `std::option::Option`

---

[109](https://docs.rs#109)    /// Converts from `&COption<T>` to `COption<&T>`.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    ///
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    /// # Examples
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    ///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    /// Converts an `COption<`[`String`]`>` into an `COption<`[`usize`]`>`, preserving the original.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// The [`map`] method takes the `self` argument by value, consuming the original,
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// so this technique uses `as_ref` to first take an `COption` to a reference
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// to the value inside the original.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    ///
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// [`map`]: enum.COption.html#method.map
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// [`String`]: ../../std/string/struct.String.html
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// [`usize`]: ../../std/primitive.usize.html
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    ///
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// ```ignore
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// let text: COption<String> = COption::Some("Hello, world!".to_string());
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// // First, cast `COption<String>` to `COption<&String>` with `as_ref`,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// // then consume *that* with `map`, leaving `text` on the stack.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// let text_length: COption<usize> = text.as_ref().map(|s| s.len());
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// println!("still can print text: {:?}", text);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    #[inline]
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    pub fn as_ref(&self) -> COption<&T> {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        match *self {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)            COption::Some(ref x) => COption::Some(x),
[133](https://docs.rs#133)            COption::None => COption::None,
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        }
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    /// Converts from `&mut COption<T>` to `COption<&mut T>`.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    ///
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// # Examples
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    ///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// ```ignore
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// let mut x = COption::Some(2);
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// match x.as_mut() {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    ///     COption::Some(v) => *v = 42,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    ///     COption::None => {},
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(42));
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// ```
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    #[inline]
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    pub fn as_mut(&mut self) -> COption<&mut T> {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        match *self {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            COption::Some(ref mut x) => COption::Some(x),
[153](https://docs.rs#153)            COption::None => COption::None,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        }
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    }

[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// Panics if the value is a [`COption::None`] with a custom panic message provided by
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// `msg`.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    ///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// # Examples
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    ///
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// ```ignore
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// let x = COption::Some("value");
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// assert_eq!(x.expect("the world is ending"), "value");
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    ///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// ```should_panic
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// # use solana_program_option::COption;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// x.expect("the world is ending"); // panics with `the world is ending`
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    #[inline]
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    pub fn expect(self, msg: &str) -> T {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        match self {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            COption::Some(val) => val,
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            COption::None => expect_failed(msg),
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// Moves the value `v` out of the `COption<T>` if it is [`COption::Some(v)`].
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// In general, because this function may panic, its use is discouraged.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// Instead, prefer to use pattern matching and handle the [`COption::None`]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// case explicitly.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    ///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    /// # Panics
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    ///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// Panics if the self value equals [`COption::None`].
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    ///
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    ///
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// # Examples
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// ```ignore
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// let x = COption::Some("air");
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// assert_eq!(x.unwrap(), "air");
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// ```
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    ///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// ```should_panic
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// # use solana_program_option::COption;
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// assert_eq!(x.unwrap(), "air"); // fails
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    #[inline]
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    pub fn unwrap(self) -> T {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        match self {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            COption::Some(val) => val,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            COption::None => panic!("called `COption::unwrap()` on a `COption::None` value"),
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Returns the contained value or a default.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// Arguments passed to `unwrap_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// the result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`unwrap_or_else`],
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// which is lazily evaluated.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// [`unwrap_or_else`]: #method.unwrap_or_else
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// # Examples
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    ///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// ```ignore
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some("car").unwrap_or("bike"), "car");
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.unwrap_or("bike"), "bike");
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// ```
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    #[inline]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    pub fn unwrap_or(self, def: T) -> T {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        match self {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            COption::None => def,
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// Returns the contained value or computes it from a closure.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// # Examples
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    ///
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    /// ```ignore
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// let k = 10;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(4).unwrap_or_else(|| 2 * k), 4);
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.unwrap_or_else(|| 2 * k), 20);
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// ```
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    #[inline]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    pub fn unwrap_or_else<F: FnOnce() -> T>(self, f: F) -> T {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        match self {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            COption::None => f(),
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    }

[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// Maps an `COption<T>` to `COption<U>` by applying a function to a contained value.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// # Examples
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// Converts an `COption<`[`String`]`>` into an `COption<`[`usize`]`>`, consuming the original:
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// [`String`]: ../../std/string/struct.String.html
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// [`usize`]: ../../std/primitive.usize.html
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// ```ignore
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// let maybe_some_string = COption::Some(String::from("Hello, World!"));
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// // `COption::map` takes self *by value*, consuming `maybe_some_string`
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// let maybe_some_len = maybe_some_string.map(|s| s.len());
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// assert_eq!(maybe_some_len, COption::Some(13));
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// ```
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    #[inline]
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    pub fn map<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, f: F) -> COption<U> {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        match self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            COption::Some(x) => COption::Some(f(x)),
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            COption::None => COption::None,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// Applies a function to the contained value (if any),
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// or returns the provided default (if not).
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// # Examples
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    ///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// ```ignore
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or(42, |v| v.len()), 3);
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or(42, |v| v.len()), 42);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// ```
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    #[inline]
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    pub fn map_or<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, default: U, f: F) -> U {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        match self {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            COption::Some(t) => f(t),
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            COption::None => default,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// Applies a function to the contained value (if any),
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// or computes a default (if not).
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// # Examples
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    ///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    /// ```ignore
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// let k = 21;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    ///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or_else(|| 2 * k, |v| v.len()), 3);
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    ///
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or_else(|| 2 * k, |v| v.len()), 42);
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// ```
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    #[inline]
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    pub fn map_or_else<U, D: FnOnce() -> U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, default: D, f: F) -> U {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        match self {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            COption::Some(t) => f(t),
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            COption::None => default(),
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }

[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// Transforms the `COption<T>` into a [`Result<T, E>`], mapping [`COption::Some(v)`] to
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// [`Ok(v)`] and [`COption::None`] to [`Err(err)`].
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// Arguments passed to `ok_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`ok_or_else`], which is
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// lazily evaluated.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    ///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// [`Result<T, E>`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// [`Ok(v)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// [`Err(err)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// [`ok_or_else`]: #method.ok_or_else
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// # Examples
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    ///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// ```ignore
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or(0), Ok("foo"));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    ///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or(0), Err(0));
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    #[inline]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    pub fn ok_or<E>(self, err: E) -> Result<T, E> {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        match self {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            COption::Some(v) => Ok(v),
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            COption::None => Err(err),
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Transforms the `COption<T>` into a [`Result<T, E>`], mapping [`COption::Some(v)`] to
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// [`Ok(v)`] and [`COption::None`] to [`Err(err())`].
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    ///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// [`Result<T, E>`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// [`Ok(v)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// [`Err(err())`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    ///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// # Examples

[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");

[378](https://docs.rs#378)    ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or_else(|| 0), Err(0));
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// ```
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    #[inline]
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    pub fn ok_or_else<E, F: FnOnce() -> E>(self, err: F) -> Result<T, E> {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        match self {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            COption::Some(v) => Ok(v),
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            COption::None => Err(err()),
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        }

[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// Returns [`COption::None`] if the option is [`COption::None`], otherwise calls `f` with the
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// wrapped value and returns the result.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// COption::Some languages call this operation flatmap.
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    ///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// # Examples
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    ///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// ```ignore
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// fn sq(x: u32) -> COption<u32> { COption::Some(x * x) }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// fn nope(_: u32) -> COption<u32> { COption::None }
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(sq).and_then(sq), COption::Some(16));
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(sq).and_then(nope), COption::None);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(nope).and_then(sq), COption::None);
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.and_then(sq).and_then(sq), COption::None);
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// ```
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    #[inline]
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    pub fn and_then<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> COption<U>>(self, f: F) -> COption<U> {
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        match self {
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            COption::Some(x) => f(x),
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            COption::None => COption::None,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        }
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    }
[450](https://docs.rs#450)
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// Returns [`COption::None`] if the option is [`COption::None`], otherwise calls `predicate`
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// with the wrapped value and returns:
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// - [`COption::Some(t)`] if `predicate` returns `true` (where `t` is the wrapped
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///   value), and
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// - [`COption::None`] if `predicate` returns `false`.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    ///
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// This function works similar to [`Iterator::filter()`]. You can imagine
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// the `COption<T>` being an iterator over one or zero elements. `filter()`
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// lets you decide which elements to keep.
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    ///
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// # Examples
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    ///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// ```ignore
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// fn is_even(n: &i32) -> bool {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    ///     n % 2 == 0
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// }
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    ///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.filter(is_even), COption::None);
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(3).filter(is_even), COption::None);
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(4).filter(is_even), COption::Some(4));
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    /// ```
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    ///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// [`COption::Some(t)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// [`Iterator::filter()`]: ../../std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    #[inline]
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    pub fn filter<P: FnOnce(&T) -> bool>(self, predicate: P) -> Self {
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        if let COption::Some(x) = self {
[480](https://docs.rs#480)            if predicate(&x) {
[481](https://docs.rs#481)                return COption::Some(x);
[482](https://docs.rs#482)            }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)        }
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        COption::None
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    }
[486](https://docs.rs#486)
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise returns `optb`.
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    ///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// Arguments passed to `or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    /// result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`or_else`], which is
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// lazily evaluated.
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    ///
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    /// [`or_else`]: #method.or_else
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    ///
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// # Examples
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    ///
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// ```ignore
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    /// let y = COption::None;
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    ///
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    /// let x = COption::None;
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// let y = COption::Some(100);
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(100));
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    ///
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    /// let y = COption::Some(100);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    ///
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// let y = COption::None;
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::None);
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// ```
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    #[inline]
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    pub fn or(self, optb: COption<T>) -> COption<T> {
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        match self {
[517](https://docs.rs#517)            COption::Some(_) => self,
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            COption::None => optb,
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        }
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    }

[522](https://docs.rs#522)    /// Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise calls `f` and
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    /// returns the result.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    ///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// # Examples
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    ///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// ```ignore
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// fn nobody() -> COption<&'static str> { COption::None }
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// fn vikings() -> COption<&'static str> { COption::Some("vikings") }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    ///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some("barbarians").or_else(vikings), COption::Some("barbarians"));
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(vikings), COption::Some("vikings"));
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(nobody), COption::None);
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// ```
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    #[inline]
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    pub fn or_else<F: FnOnce() -> COption<T>>(self, f: F) -> COption<T> {
[537](https://docs.rs#537)        match self {
[538](https://docs.rs#538)            COption::Some(_) => self,
[539](https://docs.rs#539)            COption::None => f(),
[540](https://docs.rs#540)        }
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    }
[542](https://docs.rs#542)
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// Returns [`COption::Some`] if exactly one of `self`, `optb` is [`COption::Some`], otherwise returns [`COption::None`].
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    ///
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    ///
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    /// # Examples
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    ///
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    /// ```ignore
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// let y: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::Some(2));
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    ///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// let y = COption::Some(2);
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::Some(2));
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    ///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// let y = COption::Some(2);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::None);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    ///
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// let y: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::None);
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// ```
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    #[inline]
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    pub fn xor(self, optb: COption<T>) -> COption<T> {
[569](https://docs.rs#569)        match (self, optb) {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)            (COption::Some(a), COption::None) => COption::Some(a),
[571](https://docs.rs#571)            (COption::None, COption::Some(b)) => COption::Some(b),
[572](https://docs.rs#572)            _ => COption::None,
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    }

[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// Inserts `v` into the option if it is [`COption::None`], then
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// returns a mutable reference to the contained value.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    ///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// # Examples
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ///
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    /// ```ignore
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    /// let mut x = COption::None;
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    ///
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    /// {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    ///     let y: &mut u32 = x.get_or_insert(5);
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    ///     assert_eq!(y, &5);
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    ///
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///     *y = 7;
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// }
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    ///
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(7));
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    /// ```
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    #[inline]
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    pub fn get_or_insert(&mut self, v: T) -> &mut T {
[601](https://docs.rs#601)        self.get_or_insert_with(|| v)
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    }
[603](https://docs.rs#603)
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    /// Inserts a value computed from `f` into the option if it is [`COption::None`], then
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// returns a mutable reference to the contained value.
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    ///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    ///
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    /// # Examples
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    ///
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    /// ```ignore
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// let mut x = COption::None;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    ///
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// {
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///     let y: &mut u32 = x.get_or_insert_with(|| 5);
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    ///     assert_eq!(y, &5);
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    ///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    ///     *y = 7;
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// }
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    ///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(7));
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    /// ```
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    #[inline]
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    pub fn get_or_insert_with<F: FnOnce() -> T>(&mut self, f: F) -> &mut T {
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        if let COption::None = *self {
[626](https://docs.rs#626)            *self = COption::Some(f())
[627](https://docs.rs#627)        }
[628](https://docs.rs#628)
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        match *self {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)            COption::Some(ref mut v) => v,
[631](https://docs.rs#631)            COption::None => unreachable!(),
[632](https://docs.rs#632)        }
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    }

[638](https://docs.rs#638)
[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// Replaces the actual value in the option by the value given in parameter,
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// returning the old value if present,
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// leaving a [`COption::Some`] in its place without deinitializing either one.
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    ///
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// # Examples
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    ///
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// ```ignore
[648](https://docs.rs#648)    /// let mut x = COption::Some(2);
[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// let old = x.replace(5);
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(5));
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    /// assert_eq!(old, COption::Some(2));
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    ///

[657](https://docs.rs#657)    /// ```

[661](https://docs.rs#661)    }

[736](https://docs.rs#736)impl<T: Default> COption<T> {
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// Returns the contained value or a default
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// Consumes the `self` argument then, if [`COption::Some`], returns the contained
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// value, otherwise if [`COption::None`], returns the [default value] for that
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// type.
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    ///
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// # Examples
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    ///
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// Converts a string to an integer, turning poorly-formed strings
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// into 0 (the default value for integers). [`parse`] converts
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    /// a string to any other type that implements [`FromStr`], returning
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// [`COption::None`] on error.
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    ///
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// ```ignore
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// let good_year_from_input = "1909";
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// let bad_year_from_input = "190blarg";
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// let good_year = good_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    /// let bad_year = bad_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    ///
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    /// assert_eq!(1909, good_year);
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    /// assert_eq!(0, bad_year);
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    /// ```
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    ///
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// [default value]: ../default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// [`parse`]: ../../std/primitive.str.html#method.parse
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    /// [`FromStr`]: ../../std/str/trait.FromStr.html
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    #[inline]
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    pub fn unwrap_or_default(self) -> T {
[767](https://docs.rs#767)        match self {
[768](https://docs.rs#768)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[769](https://docs.rs#769)            COption::None => T::default(),
[770](https://docs.rs#770)        }
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    }
[772](https://docs.rs#772)}

[774](https://docs.rs#774)impl<T: Deref> COption<T> {

[820](https://docs.rs#820)impl<T, E> COption<Result<T, E>> {
[821](https://docs.rs#821)    /// Transposes an `COption` of a [`Result`] into a [`Result`] of an `COption`.
[822](https://docs.rs#822)    ///
[823](https://docs.rs#823)    /// [`COption::None`] will be mapped to [`Ok`]`(`[`COption::None`]`)`.
[824](https://docs.rs#824)    /// [`COption::Some`]`(`[`Ok`]`(_))` and [`COption::Some`]`(`[`Err`]`(_))` will be mapped to
[825](https://docs.rs#825)    /// [`Ok`]`(`[`COption::Some`]`(_))` and [`Err`]`(_)`.
[826](https://docs.rs#826)    ///
[827](https://docs.rs#827)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[828](https://docs.rs#828)    /// [`Ok`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok
[829](https://docs.rs#829)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[830](https://docs.rs#830)    /// [`Err`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err
[831](https://docs.rs#831)    ///
[832](https://docs.rs#832)    /// # Examples
[833](https://docs.rs#833)    ///
[834](https://docs.rs#834)    /// ```ignore
[835](https://docs.rs#835)    /// #[derive(Debug, Eq, PartialEq)]
[836](https://docs.rs#836)    /// struct COption::SomeErr;
[837](https://docs.rs#837)    ///
[838](https://docs.rs#838)    /// let x: Result<COption<i32>, COption::SomeErr> = Ok(COption::Some(5));
[839](https://docs.rs#839)    /// let y: COption<Result<i32, COption::SomeErr>> = COption::Some(Ok(5));
[840](https://docs.rs#840)    /// assert_eq!(x, y.transpose());
[841](https://docs.rs#841)    /// ```
[842](https://docs.rs#842)    #[inline]
[843](https://docs.rs#843)    pub fn transpose(self) -> Result<COption<T>, E> {
[844](https://docs.rs#844)        match self {
[845](https://docs.rs#845)            COption::Some(Ok(x)) => Ok(COption::Some(x)),
[846](https://docs.rs#846)            COption::Some(Err(e)) => Err(e),
[847](https://docs.rs#847)            COption::None => Ok(COption::None),
[848](https://docs.rs#848)        }
[849](https://docs.rs#849)    }

#[repr(C)]pub enum COption<T> {

## Expand description

A C representation of Rust’s `std::option::Option`

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Returns `true` if the option is a [ COption::Some](https://docs.rs/enum.COption.html#variant.Some) value containing the given value.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#![feature(option_result_contains)]
let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(2);
assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), true);
let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(3);
assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), false);
let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), false);
```
Converts from `&COption<T>` to `COption<&T>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

Converts an `COption<``String``>` into an `COption<``usize``>`, preserving the original.
The [ map](https://docs.rs/enum.COption.html#method.map) method takes the

`self` argument by value, consuming the original,
so this technique uses `as_ref` to first take an `COption` to a reference
to the value inside the original.[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let text: COption<String> = COption::Some("Hello, world!".to_string());
// First, cast `COption<String>` to `COption<&String>` with `as_ref`,
// then consume *that* with `map`, leaving `text` on the stack.
let text_length: COption<usize> = text.as_ref().map(|s| s.len());
println!("still can print text: {:?}", text);
```
Moves the value `v` out of the `COption<T>` if it is [ COption::Some(v)](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::Some).

In general, because this function may panic, its use is discouraged.
Instead, prefer to use pattern matching and handle the [ COption::None](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None)
case explicitly.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if the self value equals [ COption::None](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

Returns the contained value or a default.

Arguments passed to `unwrap_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing
the result of a function call, it is recommended to use [ unwrap_or_else](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_or_else),
which is lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

assert_eq!(maybe_some_len, COption::Some(13));

Returns [ COption::None](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None) if the option is

[, otherwise calls](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None)

`COption::None``predicate`
with the wrapped value and returns:- `COption::Some(t)`- `predicate`returns- `true`(where- `t`is the wrapped value), and
- `COption::None`- `predicate`returns- `false`.

This function works similar to [ Iterator::filter()](https://docs.rs/std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter). You can imagine
the

`COption<T>` being an iterator over one or zero elements. `filter()`
lets you decide which elements to keep.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-16)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn is_even(n: &i32) -> bool {
    n % 2 == 0
}
assert_eq!(COption::None.filter(is_even), COption::None);
assert_eq!(COption::Some(3).filter(is_even), COption::None);
assert_eq!(COption::Some(4).filter(is_even), COption::Some(4));
```
Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise returns `optb`.

Arguments passed to `or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
result of a function call, it is recommended to use [ or_else](https://docs.rs#method.or_else), which is
lazily evaluated.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let x = COption::Some(2);
let y = COption::None;
assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
let x = COption::None;
let y = COption::Some(100);
assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(100));
let x = COption::Some(2);
let y = COption::Some(100);
assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
let y = COption::None;
assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::None);
```
Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise calls `f` and
returns the result.

assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(vikings), COption::Some("vikings"));
assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(nobody), COption::None);

Replaces the actual value in the option by the value given in parameter,
returning the old value if present,
leaving a [ COption::Some](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::Some) in its place without deinitializing either one.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let mut x = COption::Some(2);
let old = x.replace(5);
assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(5));
assert_eq!(old, COption::Some(2));
let mut x = COption::None;
let old = x.replace(3);
assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(3));
assert_eq!(old, COption::None);
```

#### pub fn [unwrap_or_default](https://docs.rs#method.unwrap_or_default)(self) -> T

Returns the contained value or a default

Consumes the `self` argument then, if [ COption::Some](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::Some), returns the contained
value, otherwise if

[, returns the](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None)

`COption::None`[default value](https://docs.rs/default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default)for that type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-27)Examples

Converts a string to an integer, turning poorly-formed strings
into 0 (the default value for integers). [ parse](https://docs.rs/std/primitive.str.html#method.parse) converts
a string to any other type that implements

[, returning](https://docs.rs/std/str/trait.FromStr.html)

`FromStr`[on error.](https://docs.rs#variant.COption::None)

`COption::None`[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
let good_year_from_input = "1909";
let bad_year_from_input = "190blarg";
let good_year = good_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
let bad_year = bad_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
assert_eq!(1909, good_year);
assert_eq!(0, bad_year);
```
Converts from `COption<T>` (or `&COption<T>`) to `COption<&T::Target>`.

Leaves the original COption in-place, creating a new one with a reference

Converts from `COption<COption<T>>` to `COption<T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

Basic usage:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#![feature(option_flattening)]
let x: COption<COption<u32>> = COption::Some(COption::Some(6));

let x: COption<COption<u32>> = COption::Some(COption::None);

```
Flattening once only removes one level of nesting:

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
#![feature(option_flattening)]
let x: COption<COption<COption<u32>>> = COption::Some(COption::Some(COption::Some(6)));
assert_eq!(COption::Some(COption::Some(6)), x.flatten());
assert_eq!(COption::Some(6), x.flatten().flatten());
```

# solana_program_option - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-program-option/latest/solana_program_option/

## Expand description

A C representation of Rust’s `Option`, used across the FFI
boundary for Solana program interfaces.

This implementation mostly matches `std::option` except iterators since the iteration
trait requires returning `std::option::Option`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [COption](https://docs.rs/enum.COption.html)
- A C representation of Rust’s `std::option::Option`

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-option/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |

# borsh - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/borsh/^1.5.5/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

[§](https://docs.rs#ecosystem-features)Ecosystem features

-
**std**- When enabled,`borsh`uses the standard library. Disabling this feature will result in building the crate in`no_std`environment.To carter such builds, Borsh offers `io``BorshSerialize``BorshDeserialize``io::Read`,`io::Write`and`io::Result`.When **std**feature is enabled, those items are re-exports of corresponding`std::io`items. Otherwise they are borsh-specific types which mimic behaviour of corresponding standard types.

[§](https://docs.rs#default-features)Default features

- **std**- enabled by default.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

-
**derive**- Gates derive macros of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)traits.
-
**unstable__schema**- Gates[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)trait and its derive macro. Gates[schema](https://docs.rs/schema/index.html)module. This feature requires**derive**to be enabled too.
-
**rc**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for`Rc<T>``Arc<T>``no_std`setting`Rc`/`Arc`are pulled from`alloc`crate. Serializing and deserializing these types does not preserve identity and may result in multiple copies of the same data. Be sure that this is what you want before enabling this feature.
-
**hashbrown**- Pulls in[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)when no`std`is available. This feature is set to be mutually exclusive with**std**feature.
-
**bytes**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[Bytes](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.Bytes.html)and[BytesMut](https://docs.rs/bytes/1.5.0/bytes/struct.BytesMut.html). In`no_std`builds this keeps`bytes`in`no_std`mode; when**std**is enabled,`bytes/std`is enabled as well.
-
**bson**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[ObjectId](https://docs.rs/bson/2.9.0/bson/oid/struct.ObjectId.html).
-
**indexmap**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html)and[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)for[indexmap::IndexMap](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/map/struct.IndexMap.html)and[IndexSet](https://docs.rs/indexmap/2.8.0/indexmap/set/struct.IndexSet.html)
-
**ascii**- Gates implementation of[BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),[BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html),[BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for types from[ascii](https://docs.rs/ascii/1.1.0/ascii/)crate.
-
**de_strict_order**- Enables check that keys, parsed during deserialization of[HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/[HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html)and[BTreeSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/set/struct.BTreeSet.html)/[BTreeMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/collections/btree/map/struct.BTreeMap.html)are encountered in ascending order with respect to[PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html)for hash collections, and[Ord](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.Ord.html)for btree ones. Deserialization emits error otherwise.If this feature is not enabled, it is possible that two different byte slices could deserialize into the same `HashMap`/`HashSet`object.

[§](https://docs.rs#config-aliases)Config aliases

- **hash_collections**- This is a feature alias, set up in- `build.rs`to be equivalent to (- **std**OR- **hashbrown**). Gates implementation of- [BorshSerialize](https://docs.rs/ser/trait.BorshSerialize.html),- [BorshDeserialize](https://docs.rs/de/trait.BorshDeserialize.html)and- [BorshSchema](https://docs.rs/schema/trait.BorshSchema.html)for- [HashMap](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/map/struct.HashMap.html)/- [HashSet](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/collections/hash/set/struct.HashSet.html).

# bytemuck - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bytemuck/^1.21.0/

## Expand description

This crate gives small utilities for casting between plain data types.

[§](https://docs.rs#basics)Basics

Data comes in five basic forms in Rust, so we have five basic casting functions:

- `T`uses- `cast`
- `&T`uses- `cast_ref`
- `&mut T`uses- `cast_mut`
- `&[T]`uses- `cast_slice`
- `&mut [T]`uses- `cast_slice_mut`

Depending on the function, the [ NoUninit](https://docs.rs/trait.NoUninit.html) and/or

[traits are used to maintain memory safety.](https://docs.rs/trait.AnyBitPattern.html)

`AnyBitPattern`**Historical Note:** When the crate first started the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait was used
instead, and so you may hear people refer to that, but it has the strongest
requirements and people eventually wanted the more fine-grained system, so
here we are. All types that impl

`Pod` have a blanket impl to also support
`NoUninit` and `AnyBitPattern`. The traits unfortunately do not have a
perfectly clean hierarchy for semver reasons.[§](https://docs.rs#failures)Failures

Some casts will never fail, and other casts might fail.

- `cast::<u32, f32>`always works (and- `f32::from_bits`
- `cast_ref::<[u8; 4], u32>`might fail if the specific array reference given at runtime doesn’t have alignment 4.

In addition to the “normal” forms of each function, which will panic on
invalid input, there’s also `try_` versions which will return a `Result`.

If you would like to statically ensure that a cast will work at runtime you
can use the `must_cast` crate feature and the `must_` casting functions. A
“must cast” that can’t be statically known to be valid will cause a
compilation error (and sometimes a very hard to read compilation error).

[§](https://docs.rs#using-your-own-types)Using Your Own Types

All the functions listed above are guarded by the [ Pod](https://docs.rs/trait.Pod.html) trait, which is a
sub-trait of the

[trait.](https://docs.rs/trait.Zeroable.html)

`Zeroable`If you enable the crate’s `derive` feature then these traits can be derived
on your own types. The derive macros will perform the necessary checks on
your type declaration, and trigger an error if your type does not qualify.

The derive macros might not cover all edge cases, and sometimes they will
error when actually everything is fine. As a last resort you can impl these
traits manually. However, these traits are `unsafe`, and you should
carefully read the requirements before using a manual implementation.

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

The crate supports Rust 1.34 when no features are enabled, and so there’s cargo features for thing that you might consider “obvious”.

The cargo features **do not** promise any particular MSRV, and they may
increase their MSRV in new versions.

- `derive`: Provide derive macros for the various traits.
- `extern_crate_alloc`: Provide utilities for- `alloc`related types such as Box and Vec.
- `zeroable_maybe_uninit`and- `zeroable_atomics`: Provide more- `Zeroable`
- `pod_saturating`: Provide more- `Pod`- `Zeroable`
- `wasm_simd`and- `aarch64_simd`: Support more SIMD types.
- `min_const_generics`: Provides appropriate impls for arrays of all lengths instead of just for a select list of array lengths.
- `must_cast`: Provides the- `must_`functions, which will compile error if the requested cast can’t be statically verified.
- `const_zeroed`: Provides a const version of the- `zeroed`function.

[§](https://docs.rs#related-crates)Related Crates

- `pack1`- `bytemuck`-compatible packed little-endian, big-endian and native-endian integer and floating point number types.
