# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.226/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)

- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)

# serde_with - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_with/^3.12.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides custom de/serialization helpers to use in combination with [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with) and with the improved

[-annotation. Some common use cases are:](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/serde_as/index.html)

`serde_as`- De/Serializing a type using the `Display`and`FromStr`traits, e.g., for`u8`,`url::Url`, or`mime::Mime`. Check`DisplayFromStr`
- Support for arrays larger than 32 elements or using const generics.
With `serde_as`large arrays are supported, even if they are nested in other types.`[bool; 64]`,`Option<[u8; M]>`, and`Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>`are all supported, as[this examples shows](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays).
- Skip serializing all empty `Option`types with`#[skip_serializing_none]`
- Apply a prefix / suffix to each field name of a struct, without changing the de/serialize implementations of the struct using `with_prefix!``with_suffix!`
- Deserialize a comma separated list like `#hash,#tags,#are,#great`into a`Vec<String>`. Check the documentation for`serde_with::StringWithSeparator::<CommaSeparator, T>`

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-help)Getting Help

**Check out the  user guide to find out more tips and tricks about this crate.**

For further help using this crate you can [open a new discussion](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/discussions/new) or ask on [users.rust-lang.org](https://users.rust-lang.org/).
For bugs, please open a [new issue](https://github.com/jonasbb/serde_with/issues/new) on GitHub.

[§](https://docs.rs#use-serde_with-in-your-project)Use `serde_with` in your Project

```
# Add the current version to your Cargo.toml
cargo add serde_with
```
The crate contains different features for integration with other common crates.
Check the [feature flags](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/feature_flags/index.html) section for information about all available features.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Annotate your struct or enum to enable the custom de/serializer.
The `#[serde_as]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

The `as` is analogous to the `with` attribute of serde.
You mirror the type structure of the field you want to de/serialize.
You can specify converters for the inner types of a field, e.g., `Vec<DisplayFromStr>`.
The default de/serialization behavior can be restored by using `_` as a placeholder, e.g., `BTreeMap<_, DisplayFromStr>`.

[§](https://docs.rs#displayfromstr)`DisplayFromStr`

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    // Serialize with Display, deserialize with FromStr
    #[serde_as(as = "DisplayFromStr")]
    bar: u8,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {bar: 12}
// into this JSON
{"bar": "12"}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#large-and-const-generic-arrays)Large and const-generic arrays

serde does not support arrays with more than 32 elements or using const-generics.
The `serde_as` attribute allows circumventing this restriction, even for nested types and nested arrays.

On top of it, `[u8; N]` (aka, bytes) can use the specialized `"Bytes"` for efficiency much like the `serde_bytes` crate.

```
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Arrays<const N: usize, const M: usize> {
    #[serde_as(as = "[_; N]")]
    constgeneric: [bool; N],
    #[serde_as(as = "Box<[[_; 64]; N]>")]
    nested: Box<[[u8; 64]; N]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Option<[_; M]>")]
    optional: Option<[u8; M]>,
    #[serde_as(as = "Bytes")]
    bytes: [u8; M],
}
// This allows us to serialize a struct like this
let arrays: Arrays<100, 128> = Arrays {
    constgeneric: [true; 100],
    nested: Box::new([[111; 64]; 100]),
    optional: Some([222; 128]),
    bytes: [0x42; 128],
};
assert!(serde_json::to_string(&arrays).is_ok());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#skip_serializing_none)`skip_serializing_none`

This situation often occurs with JSON, but other formats also support optional fields.
If many fields are optional, putting the annotations on the structs can become tedious.
The `#[skip_serializing_none]` attribute must be placed *before* the `#[derive]`.

```
#[skip_serializing_none]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
struct Foo {
    a: Option<usize>,
    b: Option<usize>,
    c: Option<usize>,
    d: Option<usize>,
    e: Option<usize>,
    f: Option<usize>,
    g: Option<usize>,
}
// This will serialize
Foo {a: None, b: None, c: None, d: Some(4), e: None, f: None, g: Some(7)}
// into this JSON
{"d": 4, "g": 7}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#advanced-serde_as-usage)Advanced `serde_as` usage

This example is mainly supposed to highlight the flexibility of the `serde_as` annotation compared to [serde’s  with annotation](https://serde.rs/field-attrs.html#with).
More details about

`serde_as` can be found in the [user guide](https://docs.rs/serde_with/3.21.0/serde_with/guide/index.html).

```
use std::time::Duration;
#[serde_as]
#[derive(Deserialize, Serialize)]
enum Foo {
    Durations(
        // Serialize them into a list of number as seconds
        #[serde_as(as = "Vec<DurationSeconds>")]
        Vec<Duration>,
    ),
    Bytes {
        // We can treat a Vec like a map with duplicates.
        // JSON only allows string keys, so convert i32 to strings
        // The bytes will be hex encoded
        #[serde_as(as = "Map<DisplayFromStr, Hex>")]
        bytes: Vec<(i32, Vec<u8>)>,
    }
}
// This will serialize
Foo::Durations(
    vec![Duration::new(5, 0), Duration::new(3600, 0), Duration::new(0, 0)]
)
// into this JSON
{
    "Durations": [5, 3600, 0]
}
// and serializes
Foo::Bytes {
    bytes: vec![
        (1, vec![0, 1, 2]),
        (-100, vec![100, 200, 255]),
        (1, vec![0, 111, 222]),
    ],
}
// into this JSON
{
    "Bytes": {
        "bytes": {
            "1": "000102",
            "-100": "64c8ff",
            "1": "006fde"
        }
    }
}
```

# wincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/wincode/^0.5.0/

## Expand description

wincode is a fast, bincode‑compatible serializer/deserializer focused on in‑place initialization and direct memory writes.

In short, `wincode` operates over traits that facilitate direct writes of memory
into final destinations (including heap-allocated buffers) without intermediate
staging buffers.

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

`wincode` traits are implemented for many built-in types (like `Vec`, integers, etc.).

You’ll most likely want to start by using `wincode` on your own struct types, which can be
done easily with the derive macros.

```
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct MyStruct {
    data: Vec<u8>,
    win: bool,
}
let val = MyStruct { data: vec![1,2,3], win: true };
assert_eq!(wincode::serialize(&val).unwrap(), bincode::serialize(&val).unwrap());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#motivation)Motivation

Typical Rust API design employs a *construct-then-move* style of programming.
Common APIs like `Vec::push`, iterator adaptors, `Box::new` (and its `Rc`/`Arc`
variants), and even returning a fully-initialized struct from a function all
follow this pattern. While this style feels intuitive and ergonomic, it
inherently entails copying unless the compiler can perform elision – which,
today, it generally cannot. To see why this is a consequence of the design,
consider the following code:

`Box::new(MyStruct::new());``MyStruct` must be constructed *before* it can be moved into `Box`’s allocation.
This is a classic code ordering problem: to avoid the copy, `Box::new` needs
to execute code before `MyStruct::new()` runs. `Vec::push`, iterator collection,
and similar APIs have this same problem.
(See these [design meeting notes](https://hackmd.io/XXuVXH46T8StJB_y0urnYg) or
or the
[ placement-by-return RFC](https://github.com/PoignardAzur/rust-rfcs/blob/placement-by-return/text/0000-placement-by-return.md)
for a more in-depth discussion on this topic.) The result of this is that even
performance conscious developers routinely introduce avoidable copying without
realizing it.

`serde` inherits these issues since it neither attempts to
initialize in‑place nor exposes APIs to do so.These patterns are not inherent limitations of Rust, but are consequences of
conventions and APIs that do not consider in-place initialization as part of
their design. The tools for in-place construction *do* exist (see
[ MaybeUninit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/mem/maybe_uninit/union.MaybeUninit.html) and raw pointer APIs), but they are
rarely surfaced in libraries and can be cumbersome to use (see

[), so programmers are often not even aware of them or avoid them.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ptr/macro.addr_of_mut.html)

`addr_of_mut!``wincode` makes in-place initialization a first class design goal, and fundamentally
operates on [traits](https://docs.rs#traits) that facilitate direct writes of memory.

[§](https://docs.rs#adapting-foreign-types)Adapting foreign types

`wincode` can also be used to implement serialization/deserialization
on foreign types, where serialization/deserialization schemes on those types are unoptimized (and
out of your control as a foreign type). For example, consider the following struct,
defined outside of your crate:

```
use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
#[repr(transparent)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address([u8; 32]);
#[repr(transparent)]
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Hash([u8; 32]);
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
pub struct A {
    pub addresses: Vec<Address>,
    pub hash: Hash,
}
```
`serde`’s default, naive, implementation will perform per-element visitation of all bytes
in `Vec<Address>` and `Hash`. Because these fields are “plain old data”, ideally we would
avoid per-element visitation entirely and read / write these fields in a single pass.
The situation worsens if this struct needs to be written into a heap allocated data structure,
like a `Vec<A>` or `Box<[A]>`. As discussed in [motivation](https://docs.rs#motivation), all
those bytes will be initialized on the stack before being copied into the heap allocation.

`wincode` can solve this with the following:

```
mod foreign_crate {
    // Defined in some foreign crate...
    use serde::{Serialize, Deserialize};
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Clone, Copy, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct Address(pub [u8; 32]);
    #[repr(transparent)]
    #[derive(Clone, Copy, Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct Hash(pub [u8; 32]);
    #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
    pub struct A {
        pub addresses: Vec<Address>,
        pub hash: Hash,
    }
}
wincode::pod_wrapper! {
    unsafe struct PodAddress(foreign_crate::Address);
    unsafe struct PodHash(foreign_crate::Hash);
}
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[wincode(from = "foreign_crate::A")]
pub struct MyA {
    addresses: Vec<PodAddress>,
    hash: PodHash,
}
let val = foreign_crate::A {
    addresses: vec![foreign_crate::Address([0; 32]), foreign_crate::Address([1; 32])],
    hash: foreign_crate::Hash([0; 32]),
};
let bincode_serialize = bincode::serialize(&val).unwrap();
let wincode_serialize = MyA::serialize(&val).unwrap();
assert_eq!(bincode_serialize, wincode_serialize);
let bincode_deserialize: foreign_crate::A = bincode::deserialize(&bincode_serialize).unwrap();
let wincode_deserialize = MyA::deserialize(&bincode_serialize).unwrap();
assert_eq!(val, bincode_deserialize);
assert_eq!(val, wincode_deserialize);
```
Now, when deserializing `A`:

- All initialization is done in-place, including heap-allocated memory
(true of all supported contiguous heap-allocated structures in `wincode`).
- Byte fields are read and written in a single pass.

[§](https://docs.rs#compatibility)Compatibility

- Produces the same bytes as `bincode`for the covered shapes when using bincode’s default configuration, provided your`SchemaWrite``SchemaRead``containers``serde`types.
- Length encodings are pluggable via `SeqLen`
- Unlike `bincode`, this crate will fail to serialize or deserialize large dynamic data structures by default, but this can be configured. This is done for security and performance, as it allows to preallocate these data structures safely.

[§](https://docs.rs#zero-copy-deserialization)Zero-copy deserialization

`wincode`’s zero-copy deserialization is built on the following primitives:

In addition to the following on little endian targets:

Types with alignment greater than 1 can force the compiler to insert padding into your structs.
Zero-copy requires padding-free layouts; if the layout has implicit padding, `wincode` will not
qualify the type as zero-copy.

Within `wincode`, any type that is composed entirely of the above primitives is
eligible for zero-copy deserialization. This includes arrays, slices, and structs.

Structs deriving [ SchemaRead](https://docs.rs/trait.SchemaRead.html) are eligible for zero-copy deserialization
as long as they are composed entirely of the above zero-copy types, are annotated with

`#[repr(transparent)]` or `#[repr(C)]`, and have no implicit padding. Use appropriate
field ordering or add explicit padding fields if needed to eliminate implicit padding.Note that tuples are **not** eligible for zero-copy deserialization, as Rust does not
currently guarantee tuple layout.

[§](https://docs.rs#field-reordering)Field reordering

If your struct has implicit padding, you may be able to reorder fields to avoid it.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct HasPadding {
   a: u8,
   b: u32,
   c: u16,
   d: u8,
}
#[repr(C)]
struct ZeroPadding {
   b: u32,
   c: u16,
   a: u8,
   d: u8,
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#explicit-padding)Explicit padding

You may need to add an explicit padding field if reordering fields cannot yield a padding-free layout.

```
#[repr(C)]
struct HasPadding {
   a: u32,
   b: u16,
   _pad: [u8; 2],
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#u8)`&[u8]`

```
use wincode::{SchemaWrite, SchemaRead};
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct ByteRef<'a> {
    bytes: &'a [u8],
}
let bytes: Vec<u8> = vec![1, 2, 3, 4, 5];
let byte_ref = ByteRef { bytes: &bytes };
let serialized = wincode::serialize(&byte_ref).unwrap();
let deserialized: ByteRef<'_> = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(byte_ref, deserialized);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#struct-newtype)struct newtype

```
use wincode::{SchemaWrite, SchemaRead};
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[repr(transparent)]
struct Signature([u8; 64]);
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct Data<'a> {
    signature: &'a Signature,
    data: &'a [u8],
}
let signature = Signature(array::from_fn(|_| random()));
let data = Data {
    signature: &signature,
    data: &[1, 2, 3, 4, 5],
};
let serialized = wincode::serialize(&data).unwrap();
let deserialized: Data<'_> = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(data, deserialized);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#u8-n)`&[u8; N]`

```
use wincode::{SchemaWrite, SchemaRead};
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
struct HeaderRef<'a> {
    magic: &'a [u8; 7],
}
let header = HeaderRef { magic: b"W1NC0D3" };
let serialized = wincode::serialize(&header).unwrap();
let deserialized: HeaderRef<'_> = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(header, deserialized);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#in-place-mutation)In-place mutation

wincode supports in-place mutation of zero-copy types.
See [ deserialize_mut](https://docs.rs/fn.deserialize_mut.html) or

[for more details.](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroCopy.html#method.from_bytes_mut)

`ZeroCopy::from_bytes_mut`[§](https://docs.rs#zerocopy-and-configzerocopy-methods)`ZeroCopy` and `config::ZeroCopy` methods

The [ ZeroCopy](https://docs.rs/trait.ZeroCopy.html) and

[traits provide some convenience methods for working with zero-copy types.](https://docs.rs/config/trait.ZeroCopy.html)

`config::ZeroCopy`See those trait definitions for more details.

| Attribute | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `from` | `Type` | `None` | Indicates that type is a mapping from another type (example in previous section) |
| `no_suppress_unused` | `bool` | `false` | Disable unused field lints suppression. Only usable on structs with `from`. |
| `struct_extensions`(DEPRECATED) | `bool` | `false` | Generates placement initialization helpers on `SchemaRead`struct implementations. DEPRECATED; Use`#[derive(UninitBuilder)]`instead. |
| `tag_encoding` | `Type` | `None` | Specifies the encoding/decoding schema to use for the variant discriminant. Only usable on enums. |
| `assert_zero_copy` | `bool`|`Path` | `false` | Generates compile-time asserts to ensure the type meets zero-copy requirements. Can specify a custom config path, will use the if`DefaultConfig``bool`form is used. |
| `crate` | `Path` | `::wincode` | Specifies the path to the `wincode`crate. Useful when`wincode`is renamed in`Cargo.toml`or re-exported from another module. The path is emitted as written and resolved from the derive expansion site. |

[§](https://docs.rs#no_suppress_unused)`no_suppress_unused`

When creating a mapping type with `#[wincode(from = "AnotherType")]`, fields are typically
comprised of [ containers](https://docs.rs/containers/index.html) (of course not strictly always true). As a result, these structs
purely exist for the compiler to generate optimized implementations, and are never actually
constructed. As a result, unused field lints will be triggered, which can be annoying.
By default, when

`from` is used, the derive macro will generate dummy function that references all
the struct fields, which suppresses those lints. This function will ultimately be compiled out of your
build, but you can disable this by setting `no_suppress_unused` to `true`. You can also avoid
these lint errors with visibility modifiers (e.g., `pub`).Note that this only works on structs, as it is not possible to construct an arbitrary enum variant.

[§](https://docs.rs#tag_encoding)`tag_encoding`

Allows specifying the encoding/decoding schema to use for the variant discriminant. Only usable on enums.

`Deserialize` and
`Serialize` impl for your enum on the serde / bincode side.
Example:

```
use wincode::{SchemaWrite, SchemaRead};
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
#[wincode(tag_encoding = "u8")]
enum Enum {
    A,
    B,
    C,
}
assert_eq!(&wincode::serialize(&Enum::B).unwrap(), &1u8.to_le_bytes());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#field-level)Field level

| Attribute | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `with` | `Type` | `None` | Overrides the default `SchemaRead`or`SchemaWrite`implementation for the field. |
| `skip` | `bool`|`Expr` | `false` | Skips the field during serialization and deserialization (initializing with default value). |

[§](https://docs.rs#skip)`skip`

Allows omitting the field during serialization and deserialization. When type is initialized
during deserialization, the field will be set to the default value. This is typically
`Default::default()` (when using `#[wincode(skip)]` or `#[wincode(skip(default))]`), but can
be overridden by specifying `#[wincode(skip(default_val = <value>))]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant-level-enum-variants)Variant level (enum variants)

| Attribute | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `tag` | `Expr` | `None` | Specifies the discriminant expression for the variant. Only usable on enums. |

[§](https://docs.rs#tag)`tag`

Specifies the discriminant expression for the variant. Only usable on enums.

`Deserialize` and
`Serialize` impl for your enum on the serde / bincode side.
Example:

```
use wincode::{SchemaWrite, SchemaRead};
#[derive(SchemaWrite, SchemaRead)]
enum Enum {
    #[wincode(tag = 5)]
    A,
    #[wincode(tag = 8)]
    B,
    #[wincode(tag = 13)]
    C,
}
assert_eq!(&wincode::serialize(&Enum::A).unwrap(), &5u32.to_le_bytes());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#uninitbuilder)UninitBuilder

You may have some exotic serialization logic that requires you to implement `SchemaRead` manually
for a type. In these scenarios, you’ll likely want to leverage some additional helper methods
to reduce the amount of boilerplate that is typically required when dealing with uninitialized
fields.

`#[derive(UninitBuilder)]` generates a corresponding uninit builder struct for the type.
The name of the builder struct is the name of the type with `UninitBuilder` appended.
E.g., `Header` -> `HeaderUninitBuilder`.

The builder has automatic initialization tracking that does bookkeeping of which fields have been initialized.
Calling `write_<field_name>` or `read_<field_name>`, for example, will mark the field as
initialized so that it’s properly dropped if the builder is dropped on error or panic.

The builder struct has the following methods:

- `from_maybe_uninit_mut`- Creates a new builder from a mutable `MaybeUninit`reference to the type.

- Creates a new builder from a mutable
- `into_assume_init_mut`- Assumes the builder is fully initialized, drops it, and returns a mutable reference to the inner type.

- `finish`- Forgets the builder, disabling the drop logic.

- `is_init`- Checks if the builder is fully initialized by checking if all field initialization bits are set.

For each field, the builder struct provides the following methods:

- `uninit_<field_name>_mut`- Gets a mutable `MaybeUninit`projection to the`<field_name>`slot.

- Gets a mutable
- `read_<field_name>`- Reads into a `MaybeUninit`’s`<field_name>`slot from the given`Reader`

- Reads into a
- `write_<field_name>`- Writes a `MaybeUninit`’s`<field_name>`slot with the given value.

- Writes a
- `init_<field_name>_with`- Initializes the `<field_name>`slot with a given initializer function.

- Initializes the
- `assume_init_<field_name>`- Marks the `<field_name>`slot as initialized.

- Marks the

[§](https://docs.rs#safety)Safety

Correct code will call `finish` or `into_assume_init_mut` once all fields have been initialized.
Failing to do so will result in the initialized fields being dropped when the builder is dropped, which
is undefined behavior if the `MaybeUninit` is later assumed to be initialized (e.g., on successful deserialization).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
#[derive(SchemaRead, SchemaWrite, UninitBuilder)]
struct Header {
    num_required_signatures: u8,
    num_signed_accounts: u8,
    num_unsigned_accounts: u8,
}
#[derive(SchemaRead, SchemaWrite, UninitBuilder)]
struct Payload {
    header: Header,
    data: Vec<u8>,
}
#[derive(SchemaWrite, UninitBuilder)]
struct Message {
    payload: Payload,
}
// Assume for some reason we have to manually implement `SchemaRead` for `Message`.
unsafe impl<'de, C: Config> SchemaRead<'de, C> for Message {
    type Dst = Message;
    fn read(mut reader: impl Reader<'de>, dst: &mut MaybeUninit<Self::Dst>) -> ReadResult<()> {
        let mut msg_builder = MessageUninitBuilder::<C>::from_maybe_uninit_mut(dst);
        unsafe {
            msg_builder.init_payload_with(|payload| {
                // Note that the order matters here. Values are dropped in reverse
                // declaration order, and we need to ensure `header_builder` is dropped
                // before `payload_builder` in the event of an error or panic.
                let mut payload_builder = PayloadUninitBuilder::<C>::from_maybe_uninit_mut(payload);
                // payload.header will be marked as initialized if the function succeeds.
                payload_builder.init_header_with(|header| {
                    // Read directly into the projected MaybeUninit<Header> slot.
                    let mut header_builder = HeaderUninitBuilder::<C>::from_maybe_uninit_mut(header);
                    header_builder.read_num_required_signatures(reader.by_ref())?;
                    header_builder.read_num_signed_accounts(reader.by_ref())?;
                    header_builder.read_num_unsigned_accounts(reader.by_ref())?;
                    header_builder.finish();
                    Ok(())
                })?;
                // Alternatively, we could have done `payload_builder.read_header(reader.by_ref())?;`
                // rather than reading all the fields individually.
                payload_builder.read_data(reader.by_ref())?;
                // Payload is fully initialized, so we forget the builder
                // to avoid dropping the initialized fields.
                payload_builder.finish();
                Ok(())
            })?;
        }
        // Message is fully initialized.
        msg_builder.finish();
        Ok(())
    }
}
let msg = Message {
    payload: Payload {
        header: Header {
            num_required_signatures: 1,
            num_signed_accounts: 2,
            num_unsigned_accounts: 3
        },
        data: vec![4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]
    }
};
let serialized = wincode::serialize(&msg).unwrap();
let deserialized = wincode::deserialize(&serialized).unwrap();
assert_eq!(msg, deserialized);
```

# serde_json - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde_json/^1.0.139/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde-json)Serde JSON

JSON is a ubiquitous open-standard format that uses human-readable text to transmit data objects consisting of key-value pairs.

```
{
    "name": "John Doe",
    "age": 43,
    "address": {
        "street": "10 Downing Street",
        "city": "London"
    },
    "phones": [
        "+44 1234567",
        "+44 2345678"
    ]
}
```
There are three common ways that you might find yourself needing to work with JSON data in Rust.

- **As text data.**An unprocessed string of JSON data that you receive on an HTTP endpoint, read from a file, or prepare to send to a remote server.
- **As an untyped or loosely typed representation.**Maybe you want to check that some JSON data is valid before passing it on, but without knowing the structure of what it contains. Or you want to do very basic manipulations like insert a key in a particular spot.
- **As a strongly typed Rust data structure.**When you expect all or most of your data to conform to a particular structure and want to get real work done without JSON’s loosey-goosey nature tripping you up.

Serde JSON provides efficient, flexible, safe ways of converting data between each of these representations.

[§](https://docs.rs#operating-on-untyped-json-values)Operating on untyped JSON values

Any valid JSON data can be manipulated in the following recursive enum
representation. This data structure is [ serde_json::Value](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html).

```
enum Value {
    Null,
    Bool(bool),
    Number(Number),
    String(String),
    Array(Vec<Value>),
    Object(Map<String, Value>),
}
```
A string of JSON data can be parsed into a `serde_json::Value` by the
[ serde_json::from_str](https://docs.rs/fn.from_str.html) function. There is also

[for parsing from a byte slice](https://docs.rs/fn.from_slice.html)

`from_slice``&[u8]` and [for parsing from any](https://docs.rs/fn.from_reader.html)

`from_reader``io::Read` like a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde_json::{Result, Value};
fn untyped_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into serde_json::Value.
    let v: Value = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Access parts of the data by indexing with square brackets.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", v["name"], v["phones"][0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
The result of square bracket indexing like `v["name"]` is a borrow of the
data at that index, so the type is `&Value`. A JSON map can be indexed with
string keys, while a JSON array can be indexed with integer keys. If the
type of the data is not right for the type with which it is being indexed,
or if a map does not contain the key being indexed, or if the index into a
vector is out of bounds, the returned element is `Value::Null`.

When a `Value` is printed, it is printed as a JSON string. So in the code
above, the output looks like `Please call "John Doe" at the number "+44 1234567"`. The quotation marks appear because `v["name"]` is a `&Value`
containing a JSON string and its JSON representation is `"John Doe"`.
Printing as a plain string without quotation marks involves converting from
a JSON string to a Rust string with [ as_str()](https://docs.rs/enum.Value.html#method.as_str) or avoiding the use of

`Value` as described in the following section.The `Value` representation is sufficient for very basic tasks but can be
tedious to work with for anything more significant. Error handling is
verbose to implement correctly, for example imagine trying to detect the
presence of unrecognized fields in the input data. The compiler is powerless
to help you when you make a mistake, for example imagine typoing `v["name"]`
as `v["nmae"]` in one of the dozens of places it is used in your code.

[§](https://docs.rs#parsing-json-as-strongly-typed-data-structures)Parsing JSON as strongly typed data structures

Serde provides a powerful way of mapping JSON data into Rust data structures largely automatically.

```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Person {
    name: String,
    age: u8,
    phones: Vec<String>,
}
fn typed_example() -> Result<()> {
    // Some JSON input data as a &str. Maybe this comes from the user.
    let data = r#"
        {
            "name": "John Doe",
            "age": 43,
            "phones": [
                "+44 1234567",
                "+44 2345678"
            ]
        }"#;
    // Parse the string of data into a Person object. This is exactly the
    // same function as the one that produced serde_json::Value above, but
    // now we are asking it for a Person as output.
    let p: Person = serde_json::from_str(data)?;
    // Do things just like with any other Rust data structure.
    println!("Please call {} at the number {}", p.name, p.phones[0]);
    Ok(())
}
```
This is the same `serde_json::from_str` function as before, but this time we
assign the return value to a variable of type `Person` so Serde will
automatically interpret the input data as a `Person` and produce informative
error messages if the layout does not conform to what a `Person` is expected
to look like.

Any type that implements Serde’s `Deserialize` trait can be deserialized
this way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>`
and `HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Deserialize)]`.

Once we have `p` of type `Person`, our IDE and the Rust compiler can help us
use it correctly like they do for any other Rust code. The IDE can
autocomplete field names to prevent typos, which was impossible in the
`serde_json::Value` representation. And the Rust compiler can check that
when we write `p.phones[0]`, then `p.phones` is guaranteed to be a
`Vec<String>` so indexing into it makes sense and produces a `String`.

[§](https://docs.rs#constructing-json-values)Constructing JSON values

Serde JSON provides a [ json! macro](https://docs.rs/macro.json.html) to build

`serde_json::Value`
objects with very natural JSON syntax.```
use serde_json::json;
fn main() {
    // The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
    let john = json!({
        "name": "John Doe",
        "age": 43,
        "phones": [
            "+44 1234567",
            "+44 2345678"
        ]
    });
    println!("first phone number: {}", john["phones"][0]);
    // Convert to a string of JSON and print it out
    println!("{}", john.to_string());
}
```
The `Value::to_string()` function converts a `serde_json::Value` into a
`String` of JSON text.

One neat thing about the `json!` macro is that variables and expressions can
be interpolated directly into the JSON value as you are building it. Serde
will check at compile time that the value you are interpolating is able to
be represented as JSON.

```
let full_name = "John Doe";
let age_last_year = 42;
// The type of `john` is `serde_json::Value`
let john = json!({
    "name": full_name,
    "age": age_last_year + 1,
    "phones": [
        format!("+44 {}", random_phone())
    ]
});
```
This is amazingly convenient, but we have the problem we had before with
`Value`: the IDE and Rust compiler cannot help us if we get it wrong. Serde
JSON provides a better way of serializing strongly-typed data structures
into JSON text.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-json-by-serializing-data-structures)Creating JSON by serializing data structures

A data structure can be converted to a JSON string by
[ serde_json::to_string](https://docs.rs/fn.to_string.html). There is also

[which serializes to a](https://docs.rs/fn.to_vec.html)

`serde_json::to_vec``Vec<u8>` and
[which serializes to any](https://docs.rs/fn.to_writer.html)

`serde_json::to_writer``io::Write`
such as a File or a TCP stream.```
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use serde_json::Result;
#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]
struct Address {
    street: String,
    city: String,
}
fn print_an_address() -> Result<()> {
    // Some data structure.
    let address = Address {
        street: "10 Downing Street".to_owned(),
        city: "London".to_owned(),
    };
    // Serialize it to a JSON string.
    let j = serde_json::to_string(&address)?;
    // Print, write to a file, or send to an HTTP server.
    println!("{}", j);
    Ok(())
}
```
Any type that implements Serde’s `Serialize` trait can be serialized this
way. This includes built-in Rust standard library types like `Vec<T>` and
`HashMap<K, V>`, as well as any structs or enums annotated with
`#[derive(Serialize)]`.

[§](https://docs.rs#no-std-support)No-std support

As long as there is a memory allocator, it is possible to use serde_json without the rest of the Rust standard library. Disable the default “std” feature and enable the “alloc” feature:

```
[dependencies]
serde_json = { version = "1.0", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```
For JSON support in Serde without a memory allocator, please see the
[ serde-json-core](https://github.com/rust-embedded-community/serde-json-core) crate.

# MaybeNull in solana_nullable - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/solana-nullable/^1.0.0/struct.MaybeNull.html

`pub struct MaybeNull<T: `[Nullable](https://docs.rs/trait.Nullable.html)>(/* private fields */);## Expand description

A wrapper that can be used as an `Option<T>` without requiring extra space
to indicate whether the value is `Some` or `None`.

This can be used when a specific value of `T` indicates that its value is
`None`.

## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

`pub trait Nullable: `[PartialEq](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialEq.html) + [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {

# solana_program_option - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/solana-program-option/latest/target-redirect/solana_program_option/index.html

## Expand description

A C representation of Rust’s `Option`, used across the FFI
boundary for Solana program interfaces.

This implementation mostly matches `std::option` except iterators since the iteration
trait requires returning `std::option::Option`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [COption](https://docs.rs/enum.COption.html)
- A C representation of Rust’s `std::option::Option`

# solana_program_option/lib.rs

[35](https://docs.rs#35)    /// Returns `true` if the option is a [`COption::Some`] value.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)    ///
[37](https://docs.rs#37)    /// # Examples
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    ///
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    /// ```ignore
[40](https://docs.rs#40)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(2);
[41](https://docs.rs#41)    /// assert_eq!(x.is_some(), true);
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    ///
[43](https://docs.rs#43)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    /// assert_eq!(x.is_some(), false);
[45](https://docs.rs#45)    /// ```
[46](https://docs.rs#46)    ///
[47](https://docs.rs#47)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[48](https://docs.rs#48)    #[must_use = "if you intended to assert that this has a value, consider `.unwrap()` instead"]
[49](https://docs.rs#49)    #[inline]
[50](https://docs.rs#50)    pub fn is_some(&self) -> bool {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)        match *self {
[52](https://docs.rs#52)            COption::Some(_) => true,
[53](https://docs.rs#53)            COption::None => false,
[54](https://docs.rs#54)        }
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// Returns `true` if the option is a [`COption::None`] value.
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    ///
[59](https://docs.rs#59)    /// # Examples
[60](https://docs.rs#60)    ///
[61](https://docs.rs#61)    /// ```ignore
[62](https://docs.rs#62)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(2);
[63](https://docs.rs#63)    /// assert_eq!(x.is_none(), false);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)    ///
[65](https://docs.rs#65)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[66](https://docs.rs#66)    /// assert_eq!(x.is_none(), true);
[67](https://docs.rs#67)    /// ```
[68](https://docs.rs#68)    ///
[69](https://docs.rs#69)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    #[must_use = "if you intended to assert that this doesn't have a value, consider \
[71](https://docs.rs#71)                  `.and_then(|| panic!(\"`COption` had a value when expected `COption::None`\"))` instead"]
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    #[inline]
[73](https://docs.rs#73)    pub fn is_none(&self) -> bool {
[74](https://docs.rs#74)        !self.is_some()
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    }
[76](https://docs.rs#76)
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    /// Returns `true` if the option is a [`COption::Some`] value containing the given value.
[78](https://docs.rs#78)    ///
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    /// # Examples
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    ///
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// ```ignore
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    /// #![feature(option_result_contains)]
[83](https://docs.rs#83)    ///
[84](https://docs.rs#84)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(2);
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    /// assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), true);
[86](https://docs.rs#86)    ///
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::Some(3);
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    /// assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), false);
[89](https://docs.rs#89)    ///
[90](https://docs.rs#90)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[91](https://docs.rs#91)    /// assert_eq!(x.contains(&2), false);
[92](https://docs.rs#92)    /// ```
[93](https://docs.rs#93)    #[must_use]
[94](https://docs.rs#94)    #[inline]
[95](https://docs.rs#95)    pub fn contains<U>(&self, x: &U) -> bool
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    where
[97](https://docs.rs#97)        U: PartialEq<T>,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    {
[99](https://docs.rs#99)        match self {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)            COption::Some(y) => x == y,
[101](https://docs.rs#101)            COption::None => false,
[102](https://docs.rs#102)        }
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    }

[106](https://docs.rs#106)    // Adapter for working with references

[108](https://docs.rs#108)
[109](https://docs.rs#109)    /// Converts from `&COption<T>` to `COption<&T>`.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)    ///
[111](https://docs.rs#111)    /// # Examples
[112](https://docs.rs#112)    ///
[113](https://docs.rs#113)    /// Converts an `COption<`[`String`]`>` into an `COption<`[`usize`]`>`, preserving the original.
[114](https://docs.rs#114)    /// The [`map`] method takes the `self` argument by value, consuming the original,
[115](https://docs.rs#115)    /// so this technique uses `as_ref` to first take an `COption` to a reference
[116](https://docs.rs#116)    /// to the value inside the original.
[117](https://docs.rs#117)    ///
[118](https://docs.rs#118)    /// [`map`]: enum.COption.html#method.map
[119](https://docs.rs#119)    /// [`String`]: ../../std/string/struct.String.html
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    /// [`usize`]: ../../std/primitive.usize.html
[121](https://docs.rs#121)    ///
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// ```ignore
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// let text: COption<String> = COption::Some("Hello, world!".to_string());
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    /// // First, cast `COption<String>` to `COption<&String>` with `as_ref`,
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// // then consume *that* with `map`, leaving `text` on the stack.
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// let text_length: COption<usize> = text.as_ref().map(|s| s.len());
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// println!("still can print text: {:?}", text);
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    /// ```
[129](https://docs.rs#129)    #[inline]
[130](https://docs.rs#130)    pub fn as_ref(&self) -> COption<&T> {
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        match *self {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)            COption::Some(ref x) => COption::Some(x),
[133](https://docs.rs#133)            COption::None => COption::None,
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        }
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    }
[136](https://docs.rs#136)
[137](https://docs.rs#137)    /// Converts from `&mut COption<T>` to `COption<&mut T>`.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)    ///
[139](https://docs.rs#139)    /// # Examples
[140](https://docs.rs#140)    ///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    /// ```ignore
[142](https://docs.rs#142)    /// let mut x = COption::Some(2);
[143](https://docs.rs#143)    /// match x.as_mut() {
[144](https://docs.rs#144)    ///     COption::Some(v) => *v = 42,
[145](https://docs.rs#145)    ///     COption::None => {},
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    /// }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(42));
[148](https://docs.rs#148)    /// ```
[149](https://docs.rs#149)    #[inline]
[150](https://docs.rs#150)    pub fn as_mut(&mut self) -> COption<&mut T> {
[151](https://docs.rs#151)        match *self {
[152](https://docs.rs#152)            COption::Some(ref mut x) => COption::Some(x),
[153](https://docs.rs#153)            COption::None => COption::None,
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        }
[155](https://docs.rs#155)    }

[161](https://docs.rs#161)    /// Unwraps an option, yielding the content of a [`COption::Some`].
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    ///
[163](https://docs.rs#163)    /// # Panics
[164](https://docs.rs#164)    ///
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    /// Panics if the value is a [`COption::None`] with a custom panic message provided by
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    /// `msg`.
[167](https://docs.rs#167)    ///
[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    ///
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// # Examples
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    ///
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// ```ignore
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    /// let x = COption::Some("value");
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// assert_eq!(x.expect("the world is ending"), "value");
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// ```
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    ///
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// ```should_panic
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// # use solana_program_option::COption;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// x.expect("the world is ending"); // panics with `the world is ending`
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    /// ```
[183](https://docs.rs#183)    #[inline]
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    pub fn expect(self, msg: &str) -> T {
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        match self {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            COption::Some(val) => val,
[187](https://docs.rs#187)            COption::None => expect_failed(msg),
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        }
[189](https://docs.rs#189)    }
[190](https://docs.rs#190)
[191](https://docs.rs#191)    /// Moves the value `v` out of the `COption<T>` if it is [`COption::Some(v)`].
[192](https://docs.rs#192)    ///
[193](https://docs.rs#193)    /// In general, because this function may panic, its use is discouraged.
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    /// Instead, prefer to use pattern matching and handle the [`COption::None`]
[195](https://docs.rs#195)    /// case explicitly.
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    ///
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    /// # Panics
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    ///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// Panics if the self value equals [`COption::None`].
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    ///
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[202](https://docs.rs#202)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    ///
[204](https://docs.rs#204)    /// # Examples
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    ///
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// ```ignore
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// let x = COption::Some("air");
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    /// assert_eq!(x.unwrap(), "air");
[209](https://docs.rs#209)    /// ```
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    ///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    /// ```should_panic
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// # use solana_program_option::COption;
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// assert_eq!(x.unwrap(), "air"); // fails
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    /// ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    #[inline]
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    pub fn unwrap(self) -> T {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)        match self {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)            COption::Some(val) => val,
[220](https://docs.rs#220)            COption::None => panic!("called `COption::unwrap()` on a `COption::None` value"),
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        }
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Returns the contained value or a default.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    /// Arguments passed to `unwrap_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    /// the result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`unwrap_or_else`],
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// which is lazily evaluated.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    ///
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    /// [`unwrap_or_else`]: #method.unwrap_or_else
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    ///
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    /// # Examples
[233](https://docs.rs#233)    ///
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    /// ```ignore
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some("car").unwrap_or("bike"), "car");
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.unwrap_or("bike"), "bike");
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    /// ```
[238](https://docs.rs#238)    #[inline]
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    pub fn unwrap_or(self, def: T) -> T {
[240](https://docs.rs#240)        match self {
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[242](https://docs.rs#242)            COption::None => def,
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    }
[245](https://docs.rs#245)
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    /// Returns the contained value or computes it from a closure.
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    ///
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// # Examples
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    ///
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    /// ```ignore
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    /// let k = 10;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(4).unwrap_or_else(|| 2 * k), 4);
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.unwrap_or_else(|| 2 * k), 20);
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    /// ```
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    #[inline]
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    pub fn unwrap_or_else<F: FnOnce() -> T>(self, f: F) -> T {
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        match self {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            COption::None => f(),
[260](https://docs.rs#260)        }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    }

[264](https://docs.rs#264)    // Transforming contained values

[266](https://docs.rs#266)
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    /// Maps an `COption<T>` to `COption<U>` by applying a function to a contained value.
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    ///
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// # Examples
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    ///
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    /// Converts an `COption<`[`String`]`>` into an `COption<`[`usize`]`>`, consuming the original:
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    ///
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// [`String`]: ../../std/string/struct.String.html
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    /// [`usize`]: ../../std/primitive.usize.html
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// ```ignore
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// let maybe_some_string = COption::Some(String::from("Hello, World!"));
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    /// // `COption::map` takes self *by value*, consuming `maybe_some_string`
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    /// let maybe_some_len = maybe_some_string.map(|s| s.len());
[280](https://docs.rs#280)    ///
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    /// assert_eq!(maybe_some_len, COption::Some(13));
[282](https://docs.rs#282)    /// ```
[283](https://docs.rs#283)    #[inline]
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    pub fn map<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, f: F) -> COption<U> {
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        match self {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            COption::Some(x) => COption::Some(f(x)),
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            COption::None => COption::None,
[288](https://docs.rs#288)        }
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    }
[290](https://docs.rs#290)
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// Applies a function to the contained value (if any),
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    /// or returns the provided default (if not).
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    ///
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    /// # Examples
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    ///
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    /// ```ignore
[297](https://docs.rs#297)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or(42, |v| v.len()), 3);
[299](https://docs.rs#299)    ///
[300](https://docs.rs#300)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[301](https://docs.rs#301)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or(42, |v| v.len()), 42);
[302](https://docs.rs#302)    /// ```
[303](https://docs.rs#303)    #[inline]
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    pub fn map_or<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, default: U, f: F) -> U {
[305](https://docs.rs#305)        match self {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)            COption::Some(t) => f(t),
[307](https://docs.rs#307)            COption::None => default,
[308](https://docs.rs#308)        }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)    }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)    /// Applies a function to the contained value (if any),
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    /// or computes a default (if not).
[313](https://docs.rs#313)    ///
[314](https://docs.rs#314)    /// # Examples
[315](https://docs.rs#315)    ///
[316](https://docs.rs#316)    /// ```ignore
[317](https://docs.rs#317)    /// let k = 21;
[318](https://docs.rs#318)    ///
[319](https://docs.rs#319)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or_else(|| 2 * k, |v| v.len()), 3);
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    ///
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    /// assert_eq!(x.map_or_else(|| 2 * k, |v| v.len()), 42);
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// ```
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    #[inline]
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    pub fn map_or_else<U, D: FnOnce() -> U, F: FnOnce(T) -> U>(self, default: D, f: F) -> U {
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        match self {
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            COption::Some(t) => f(t),
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            COption::None => default(),
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        }
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    }
[332](https://docs.rs#332)
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// Transforms the `COption<T>` into a [`Result<T, E>`], mapping [`COption::Some(v)`] to
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// [`Ok(v)`] and [`COption::None`] to [`Err(err)`].
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    ///
[336](https://docs.rs#336)    /// Arguments passed to `ok_or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    /// result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`ok_or_else`], which is
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    /// lazily evaluated.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    ///
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    /// [`Result<T, E>`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    /// [`Ok(v)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// [`Err(err)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[344](https://docs.rs#344)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// [`ok_or_else`]: #method.ok_or_else
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    ///
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    /// # Examples
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    ///
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// ```ignore
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or(0), Ok("foo"));
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    ///
[353](https://docs.rs#353)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or(0), Err(0));
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    /// ```
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    #[inline]
[357](https://docs.rs#357)    pub fn ok_or<E>(self, err: E) -> Result<T, E> {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)        match self {
[359](https://docs.rs#359)            COption::Some(v) => Ok(v),
[360](https://docs.rs#360)            COption::None => Err(err),
[361](https://docs.rs#361)        }
[362](https://docs.rs#362)    }
[363](https://docs.rs#363)
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Transforms the `COption<T>` into a [`Result<T, E>`], mapping [`COption::Some(v)`] to
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// [`Ok(v)`] and [`COption::None`] to [`Err(err())`].
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    ///
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    /// [`Result<T, E>`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// [`Ok(v)`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// [`Err(err())`]: ../../std/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// [`COption::Some(v)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    ///
[373](https://docs.rs#373)    /// # Examples
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    ///
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    /// ```ignore
[376](https://docs.rs#376)    /// let x = COption::Some("foo");
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or_else(|| 0), Ok("foo"));
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    ///
[379](https://docs.rs#379)    /// let x: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[380](https://docs.rs#380)    /// assert_eq!(x.ok_or_else(|| 0), Err(0));
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    /// ```
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    #[inline]
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    pub fn ok_or_else<E, F: FnOnce() -> E>(self, err: F) -> Result<T, E> {
[384](https://docs.rs#384)        match self {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)            COption::Some(v) => Ok(v),
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            COption::None => Err(err()),
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        }
[388](https://docs.rs#388)    }
[389](https://docs.rs#389)

[394](https://docs.rs#394)    /// Returns [`COption::None`] if the option is [`COption::None`], otherwise returns `optb`.
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    ///
[396](https://docs.rs#396)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    ///
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// # Examples
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    ///
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// ```ignore
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[402](https://docs.rs#402)    /// let y: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[403](https://docs.rs#403)    /// assert_eq!(x.and(y), COption::None);
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    ///
[405](https://docs.rs#405)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// let y = COption::Some("foo");
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// assert_eq!(x.and(y), COption::None);
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    ///
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    /// let y = COption::Some("foo");
[411](https://docs.rs#411)    /// assert_eq!(x.and(y), COption::Some("foo"));
[412](https://docs.rs#412)    ///
[413](https://docs.rs#413)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    /// let y: COption<&str> = COption::None;
[415](https://docs.rs#415)    /// assert_eq!(x.and(y), COption::None);
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    /// ```
[417](https://docs.rs#417)    #[inline]
[418](https://docs.rs#418)    pub fn and<U>(self, optb: COption<U>) -> COption<U> {
[419](https://docs.rs#419)        match self {
[420](https://docs.rs#420)            COption::Some(_) => optb,
[421](https://docs.rs#421)            COption::None => COption::None,
[422](https://docs.rs#422)        }
[423](https://docs.rs#423)    }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)
[425](https://docs.rs#425)    /// Returns [`COption::None`] if the option is [`COption::None`], otherwise calls `f` with the
[426](https://docs.rs#426)    /// wrapped value and returns the result.
[427](https://docs.rs#427)    ///
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// COption::Some languages call this operation flatmap.
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    ///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    ///
[432](https://docs.rs#432)    /// # Examples
[433](https://docs.rs#433)    ///
[434](https://docs.rs#434)    /// ```ignore
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    /// fn sq(x: u32) -> COption<u32> { COption::Some(x * x) }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)    /// fn nope(_: u32) -> COption<u32> { COption::None }
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    ///
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(sq).and_then(sq), COption::Some(16));
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(sq).and_then(nope), COption::None);
[440](https://docs.rs#440)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(2).and_then(nope).and_then(sq), COption::None);
[441](https://docs.rs#441)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.and_then(sq).and_then(sq), COption::None);
[442](https://docs.rs#442)    /// ```
[443](https://docs.rs#443)    #[inline]
[444](https://docs.rs#444)    pub fn and_then<U, F: FnOnce(T) -> COption<U>>(self, f: F) -> COption<U> {
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        match self {
[446](https://docs.rs#446)            COption::Some(x) => f(x),
[447](https://docs.rs#447)            COption::None => COption::None,
[448](https://docs.rs#448)        }
[449](https://docs.rs#449)    }
[450](https://docs.rs#450)
[451](https://docs.rs#451)    /// Returns [`COption::None`] if the option is [`COption::None`], otherwise calls `predicate`
[452](https://docs.rs#452)    /// with the wrapped value and returns:
[453](https://docs.rs#453)    ///
[454](https://docs.rs#454)    /// - [`COption::Some(t)`] if `predicate` returns `true` (where `t` is the wrapped
[455](https://docs.rs#455)    ///   value), and
[456](https://docs.rs#456)    /// - [`COption::None`] if `predicate` returns `false`.
[457](https://docs.rs#457)    ///
[458](https://docs.rs#458)    /// This function works similar to [`Iterator::filter()`]. You can imagine
[459](https://docs.rs#459)    /// the `COption<T>` being an iterator over one or zero elements. `filter()`
[460](https://docs.rs#460)    /// lets you decide which elements to keep.
[461](https://docs.rs#461)    ///
[462](https://docs.rs#462)    /// # Examples
[463](https://docs.rs#463)    ///
[464](https://docs.rs#464)    /// ```ignore
[465](https://docs.rs#465)    /// fn is_even(n: &i32) -> bool {
[466](https://docs.rs#466)    ///     n % 2 == 0
[467](https://docs.rs#467)    /// }
[468](https://docs.rs#468)    ///
[469](https://docs.rs#469)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.filter(is_even), COption::None);
[470](https://docs.rs#470)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(3).filter(is_even), COption::None);
[471](https://docs.rs#471)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some(4).filter(is_even), COption::Some(4));
[472](https://docs.rs#472)    /// ```
[473](https://docs.rs#473)    ///
[474](https://docs.rs#474)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[475](https://docs.rs#475)    /// [`COption::Some(t)`]: #variant.COption::Some
[476](https://docs.rs#476)    /// [`Iterator::filter()`]: ../../std/iter/trait.Iterator.html#method.filter
[477](https://docs.rs#477)    #[inline]
[478](https://docs.rs#478)    pub fn filter<P: FnOnce(&T) -> bool>(self, predicate: P) -> Self {
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        if let COption::Some(x) = self {
[480](https://docs.rs#480)            if predicate(&x) {
[481](https://docs.rs#481)                return COption::Some(x);
[482](https://docs.rs#482)            }
[483](https://docs.rs#483)        }
[484](https://docs.rs#484)        COption::None
[485](https://docs.rs#485)    }
[486](https://docs.rs#486)
[487](https://docs.rs#487)    /// Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise returns `optb`.
[488](https://docs.rs#488)    ///
[489](https://docs.rs#489)    /// Arguments passed to `or` are eagerly evaluated; if you are passing the
[490](https://docs.rs#490)    /// result of a function call, it is recommended to use [`or_else`], which is
[491](https://docs.rs#491)    /// lazily evaluated.
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    ///
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    /// [`or_else`]: #method.or_else
[494](https://docs.rs#494)    ///
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    /// # Examples
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    ///
[497](https://docs.rs#497)    /// ```ignore
[498](https://docs.rs#498)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[499](https://docs.rs#499)    /// let y = COption::None;
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    ///
[502](https://docs.rs#502)    /// let x = COption::None;
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    /// let y = COption::Some(100);
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(100));
[505](https://docs.rs#505)    ///
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    /// let y = COption::Some(100);
[508](https://docs.rs#508)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::Some(2));
[509](https://docs.rs#509)    ///
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[511](https://docs.rs#511)    /// let y = COption::None;
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    /// assert_eq!(x.or(y), COption::None);
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    /// ```
[514](https://docs.rs#514)    #[inline]
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    pub fn or(self, optb: COption<T>) -> COption<T> {
[516](https://docs.rs#516)        match self {
[517](https://docs.rs#517)            COption::Some(_) => self,
[518](https://docs.rs#518)            COption::None => optb,
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        }
[520](https://docs.rs#520)    }
[521](https://docs.rs#521)
[522](https://docs.rs#522)    /// Returns the option if it contains a value, otherwise calls `f` and
[523](https://docs.rs#523)    /// returns the result.
[524](https://docs.rs#524)    ///
[525](https://docs.rs#525)    /// # Examples
[526](https://docs.rs#526)    ///
[527](https://docs.rs#527)    /// ```ignore
[528](https://docs.rs#528)    /// fn nobody() -> COption<&'static str> { COption::None }
[529](https://docs.rs#529)    /// fn vikings() -> COption<&'static str> { COption::Some("vikings") }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    ///
[531](https://docs.rs#531)    /// assert_eq!(COption::Some("barbarians").or_else(vikings), COption::Some("barbarians"));
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(vikings), COption::Some("vikings"));
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    /// assert_eq!(COption::None.or_else(nobody), COption::None);
[534](https://docs.rs#534)    /// ```
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    #[inline]
[536](https://docs.rs#536)    pub fn or_else<F: FnOnce() -> COption<T>>(self, f: F) -> COption<T> {
[537](https://docs.rs#537)        match self {
[538](https://docs.rs#538)            COption::Some(_) => self,
[539](https://docs.rs#539)            COption::None => f(),
[540](https://docs.rs#540)        }
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    }
[542](https://docs.rs#542)
[543](https://docs.rs#543)    /// Returns [`COption::Some`] if exactly one of `self`, `optb` is [`COption::Some`], otherwise returns [`COption::None`].
[544](https://docs.rs#544)    ///
[545](https://docs.rs#545)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[546](https://docs.rs#546)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[547](https://docs.rs#547)    ///
[548](https://docs.rs#548)    /// # Examples
[549](https://docs.rs#549)    ///
[550](https://docs.rs#550)    /// ```ignore
[551](https://docs.rs#551)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[552](https://docs.rs#552)    /// let y: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[553](https://docs.rs#553)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::Some(2));
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    ///
[555](https://docs.rs#555)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[556](https://docs.rs#556)    /// let y = COption::Some(2);
[557](https://docs.rs#557)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::Some(2));
[558](https://docs.rs#558)    ///
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    /// let x = COption::Some(2);
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// let y = COption::Some(2);
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::None);
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    ///
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// let x: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// let y: COption<u32> = COption::None;
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// assert_eq!(x.xor(y), COption::None);
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// ```
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    #[inline]
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    pub fn xor(self, optb: COption<T>) -> COption<T> {
[569](https://docs.rs#569)        match (self, optb) {
[570](https://docs.rs#570)            (COption::Some(a), COption::None) => COption::Some(a),
[571](https://docs.rs#571)            (COption::None, COption::Some(b)) => COption::Some(b),
[572](https://docs.rs#572)            _ => COption::None,
[573](https://docs.rs#573)        }
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    }

[580](https://docs.rs#580)    /// Inserts `v` into the option if it is [`COption::None`], then
[581](https://docs.rs#581)    /// returns a mutable reference to the contained value.
[582](https://docs.rs#582)    ///
[583](https://docs.rs#583)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[584](https://docs.rs#584)    ///
[585](https://docs.rs#585)    /// # Examples
[586](https://docs.rs#586)    ///
[587](https://docs.rs#587)    /// ```ignore
[588](https://docs.rs#588)    /// let mut x = COption::None;
[589](https://docs.rs#589)    ///
[590](https://docs.rs#590)    /// {
[591](https://docs.rs#591)    ///     let y: &mut u32 = x.get_or_insert(5);
[592](https://docs.rs#592)    ///     assert_eq!(y, &5);
[593](https://docs.rs#593)    ///
[594](https://docs.rs#594)    ///     *y = 7;
[595](https://docs.rs#595)    /// }
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    ///
[597](https://docs.rs#597)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(7));
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    /// ```
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    #[inline]
[600](https://docs.rs#600)    pub fn get_or_insert(&mut self, v: T) -> &mut T {
[601](https://docs.rs#601)        self.get_or_insert_with(|| v)
[602](https://docs.rs#602)    }
[603](https://docs.rs#603)
[604](https://docs.rs#604)    /// Inserts a value computed from `f` into the option if it is [`COption::None`], then
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    /// returns a mutable reference to the contained value.
[606](https://docs.rs#606)    ///
[607](https://docs.rs#607)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[608](https://docs.rs#608)    ///
[609](https://docs.rs#609)    /// # Examples
[610](https://docs.rs#610)    ///
[611](https://docs.rs#611)    /// ```ignore
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    /// let mut x = COption::None;
[613](https://docs.rs#613)    ///
[614](https://docs.rs#614)    /// {
[615](https://docs.rs#615)    ///     let y: &mut u32 = x.get_or_insert_with(|| 5);
[616](https://docs.rs#616)    ///     assert_eq!(y, &5);
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    ///
[618](https://docs.rs#618)    ///     *y = 7;
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    /// }
[620](https://docs.rs#620)    ///
[621](https://docs.rs#621)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(7));
[622](https://docs.rs#622)    /// ```
[623](https://docs.rs#623)    #[inline]
[624](https://docs.rs#624)    pub fn get_or_insert_with<F: FnOnce() -> T>(&mut self, f: F) -> &mut T {
[625](https://docs.rs#625)        if let COption::None = *self {
[626](https://docs.rs#626)            *self = COption::Some(f())
[627](https://docs.rs#627)        }
[628](https://docs.rs#628)
[629](https://docs.rs#629)        match *self {
[630](https://docs.rs#630)            COption::Some(ref mut v) => v,
[631](https://docs.rs#631)            COption::None => unreachable!(),
[632](https://docs.rs#632)        }
[633](https://docs.rs#633)    }

[639](https://docs.rs#639)    /// Replaces the actual value in the option by the value given in parameter,
[640](https://docs.rs#640)    /// returning the old value if present,
[641](https://docs.rs#641)    /// leaving a [`COption::Some`] in its place without deinitializing either one.
[642](https://docs.rs#642)    ///
[643](https://docs.rs#643)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[644](https://docs.rs#644)    ///
[645](https://docs.rs#645)    /// # Examples
[646](https://docs.rs#646)    ///
[647](https://docs.rs#647)    /// ```ignore

[649](https://docs.rs#649)    /// let old = x.replace(5);
[650](https://docs.rs#650)    /// assert_eq!(x, COption::Some(5));
[651](https://docs.rs#651)    /// assert_eq!(old, COption::Some(2));
[652](https://docs.rs#652)    ///
[653](https://docs.rs#653)    /// let mut x = COption::None;
[654](https://docs.rs#654)    /// let old = x.replace(3);

[656](https://docs.rs#656)    /// assert_eq!(old, COption::None);
[657](https://docs.rs#657)    /// ```
[658](https://docs.rs#658)    #[inline]
[659](https://docs.rs#659)    pub fn replace(&mut self, value: T) -> COption<T> {
[660](https://docs.rs#660)        mem::replace(self, COption::Some(value))
[661](https://docs.rs#661)    }

[736](https://docs.rs#736)impl<T: Default> COption<T> {
[737](https://docs.rs#737)    /// Returns the contained value or a default
[738](https://docs.rs#738)    ///
[739](https://docs.rs#739)    /// Consumes the `self` argument then, if [`COption::Some`], returns the contained
[740](https://docs.rs#740)    /// value, otherwise if [`COption::None`], returns the [default value] for that
[741](https://docs.rs#741)    /// type.
[742](https://docs.rs#742)    ///
[743](https://docs.rs#743)    /// # Examples
[744](https://docs.rs#744)    ///
[745](https://docs.rs#745)    /// Converts a string to an integer, turning poorly-formed strings
[746](https://docs.rs#746)    /// into 0 (the default value for integers). [`parse`] converts
[747](https://docs.rs#747)    /// a string to any other type that implements [`FromStr`], returning
[748](https://docs.rs#748)    /// [`COption::None`] on error.
[749](https://docs.rs#749)    ///
[750](https://docs.rs#750)    /// ```ignore
[751](https://docs.rs#751)    /// let good_year_from_input = "1909";
[752](https://docs.rs#752)    /// let bad_year_from_input = "190blarg";
[753](https://docs.rs#753)    /// let good_year = good_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
[754](https://docs.rs#754)    /// let bad_year = bad_year_from_input.parse().ok().unwrap_or_default();
[755](https://docs.rs#755)    ///
[756](https://docs.rs#756)    /// assert_eq!(1909, good_year);
[757](https://docs.rs#757)    /// assert_eq!(0, bad_year);
[758](https://docs.rs#758)    /// ```
[759](https://docs.rs#759)    ///
[760](https://docs.rs#760)    /// [`COption::Some`]: #variant.COption::Some
[761](https://docs.rs#761)    /// [`COption::None`]: #variant.COption::None
[762](https://docs.rs#762)    /// [default value]: ../default/trait.Default.html#tymethod.default
[763](https://docs.rs#763)    /// [`parse`]: ../../std/primitive.str.html#method.parse
[764](https://docs.rs#764)    /// [`FromStr`]: ../../std/str/trait.FromStr.html
[765](https://docs.rs#765)    #[inline]
[766](https://docs.rs#766)    pub fn unwrap_or_default(self) -> T {
[767](https://docs.rs#767)        match self {
[768](https://docs.rs#768)            COption::Some(x) => x,
[769](https://docs.rs#769)            COption::None => T::default(),
[770](https://docs.rs#770)        }
[771](https://docs.rs#771)    }
